text:
RIYADH: A more than 2 billion Egyptian pound ($39 million) investment will be used to establish an electric-battery manufacturing plant in Egypt by local battery maker BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd., as the country seeks to develop its electric-vehicle industry and expand local manufacturing.

The plant will initially have production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour a year, with output focused on batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, according to a government statement.

The second phase will expand production to passenger-vehicle batteries and energy-storage systems for solar and wind power, taking total capacity to 5 GWh annually and targeting a 40 percent local-content ratio.

Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly witnessed the signing of the contract to establish the factory, which will produce various types of electric batteries, according to the government statement. The agreement was signed by Maged Wahib, chairman of BME, and Luo Haining, CATL’s director of international investment. Egypt’s Industry Minister Khaled Hashem attended the signing, along with BME project manager Amin Karim Ghabbour and board member Lotfy Tadros.

The project comes as Egypt seeks to deepen local automotive manufacturing and establish itself as a regional production hub. The country’s National Industrial Strategy 2026-2030 identifies automotive manufacturing, electrical and engineering industries and electronics among seven priority sectors, while targeting $100 billion in non-oil exports by 2030, according to the Presidency.

Egypt is also expanding renewable-energy generation and battery storage. The government aims to raise renewable sources to 45 percent of electricity generation by 2028, while battery-storage additions are planned to increase grid capacity using the technology to about 1.1 GW.

The government statement said: “The new plant aims to establish a specialized industrial base for battery systems in Egypt.” Production will initially focus on heavy commercial vehicles, with the second phase covering passenger-vehicle batteries and energy-storage systems for solar and wind power.

The project is intended to serve both local and international markets, while creating jobs and developing technical skills for Egypt’s labor force. “The project aims to meet the demands of both local and global markets for electric batteries, while also creating job opportunities and enhancing the skills of technical personnel for the Egyptian labor market,” the statement said.

The partnership will combine BME’s Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities with CATL’s battery technology, production equipment and technical support. The companies aim to manufacture battery systems that meet international quality and production standards.

Locally produced batteries are expected to be supplied to vehicle manufacturers in Egypt, reducing reliance on imports as well as shipping and logistics costs. Producing batteries closer to vehicle assembly plants could also allow manufacturers to integrate the systems more closely with production lines and respond more quickly to changes in market demand.

BME was established by Egyptian commercial-vehicle manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

title: Long Before The Ford Fathom, A Dealership Sit-In Saved Ford's First Electric Pickup
description:
From 1998 through 2002, Ford would produce about 1,500 all-electric versions of its Ranger small pickup, primarily for California.
Was the Ranger EV the first-ever electric pickup?
Electric trucks can be traced back to at least 1898.
Rapid, though, was owned by GM, and its products became the basis of the GMC brand's electric trucks by 1913.
The General just beat Ford to the market with a 1997 Chevrolet S-10 pickup EV.
text:
Ford wants to somehow sell 100,000 Fathoms in its first year, and yes, that may seem a bit optimistic. But it wouldn't be the first time that the company's electric pickups inspired a passionate following. And we're not talking about the F-150 Lightning, either. From 1998 through 2002, Ford would produce about 1,500 all-electric versions of its Ranger small pickup, primarily for California. The Blue Oval only built the trucks to comply with the state's air-pollution rules at the time, which required automakers to offer a certain number of vehicles without tailpipe emissions.

Yet their owners — actually mostly lease-holders — loved them. In fact, when Ford announced it would shut down the program and take back all the trucks, it led to a full-on protest explicitly modeled on the civil-rights playbook. In this case, the result was a 2005 sit-in at Downtown Ford in Sacramento, California, where Ranger EV fans gathered for seven days of demonstrations — and got Ford to change its plans. Oh, the company was still going to cancel the EV program, even as folks were "calling on America's worst-ranked automaker to revive its EV program and immediately implement existing technology to improve the bottom-of-the-barrel fuel efficiency of the rest of its gas-guzzling fleet."

But the effort did at least save some Ranger EVs from the same crushing fate as the GM EV1. Ford decided to let then-current lease-holders purchase their trucks outright for $1, without warranty coverage. For former lessees, the company created a lottery system allowing them to buy "refurbished" trucks for $6,000 (about $12,400 today).

Read more: The Ten Dumbest Automotive Design Mistakes

Let's check the tech specs of the Ranger EV

They may be among the electric vehicles you never see anymore, but the all-electric Ford Rangers were basically the same as the gas-powered models, with obvious modifications. The onboard charger and associated hardware were under the hood instead of a gas engine, as was a radiator to help with cooling, while the battery pack was located underneath the truck and between its frame rails. As for the batteries themselves, the original setup hinvolved a 23-kWh lead-acid battery for an EPA range of 50 miles with ratings of 62 MPGe city/54 MPGe highway/58 MPGe combined. Ford would soon switch to nickel-metal hydride battery chemistry, which would raise the Ranger's travel distance to 55 miles, albeit while reducing its ratings to 50/44/47.

Oh, and the electric motor and gear-reduction system were back near the rear axle for a RWD-only driving experience supported by 90 horsepower and 140 pound-feet of torque — which compared to 112 horses and 135 pound-feet of torque in the gas Ranger's entry-level 2.3-liter I4. It was enough to get from 0 to 50 mph in about 12.5 seconds with a top speed of 75 mph, per the manufacturer. Ford also claimed a 700-pound payload — versus up to 1,650 pounds for the traditional Ranger — but does not seem to have published a maximum tow rating.

Still, the Ranger EV was tough enough for truck-style tasks, according to its owners. Those Ranger activists mentioned above were led in part by a pair of cattle ranchers, who praised its ability to pull a stuck forklift out of the mud when their diesel-powered pickup couldn't.

Was the Ranger EV the first-ever electric pickup?

Nope. Electric trucks can be traced back to at least 1898. That's when one from the Riker Motor Vehicle Company became what's considered to be New York City's first-ever all-electric delivery vehicle. Fast forward to 1911, and we find the Rapid Motor Company expanding its previous truck lineup by adding electrified models to the roster. Rapid, though, was owned by GM, and its products became the basis of the GMC brand's electric trucks by 1913. At that point, the latter had a portfolio of eight different all-electric commercial trucks ranging in price from $1,500 to $2,500.

It was then GMC's parent company — General Motors — which introduced the first all-electric pickup-style truck offered to the public by an OEM. The General just beat Ford to the market with a 1997 Chevrolet S-10 pickup EV.

The S-10 EV couldn't top its Ranger rival in most other categories, however. Like the Ford, the Chevy premiered with lead-acid batteries — but they were only good for an EPA range of 33 miles, which is less than you get with some of today's plug-in hybrids. Ford also followed Chevy's lead in offering a longer-range NiMH battery pack with a driving range of roughly 72 miles. On the other hand, the truck's efficiency ratings cratered to 28/28/28 as a result. Another result? There was a lot less customer demand, with the Bowtie brand delivering a mere 500 units or so during its two years of production. Nor was there much of an outcry to save the ultra-rare electric S-10 from the crusher. That said, a few did survive, including a trio rescued by a single person in Indiana.

name: Louisiana Environment
title: America's air monitors are disappearing. So is your power to expose polluters. | Grist
authors: Ames Alexander, Brad Racino, Floodlight, Brad Racino
description:
The decline was especially pronounced among air monitors that track toxic chemicals, including those linked to cancer and other serious health effects.
Tony Long, general counsel for the Ohio Chamber of Commerce, said businesses are concerned that uncalibrated air monitors will spread misinformation.
“You don’t want to be stopped for speeding on an uncalibrated speed gun.” With more than 90 public air monitoring stations, Ohio has a more robust air monitoring network than some states.
Yet none of Ohio’s 25 largest air polluters are within 20 miles of a public air monitoring station that measures its top toxic emission.
None of West Virginia’s 25 largest air polluters has a public air monitor within 25 miles that measures the pollutant it releases most.
text:
Across much of the U.S., people have little way to know when the air they breathe turns dangerous.

Over recent decades, federal funding for public air monitoring has declined, the number of monitors has fallen, and much of the remaining equipment is aging or located far from major polluters.

Now, the stakes are rising: Wildfire smoke is reaching more communities, data centers are adding pollution, and climate-driven heat waves are worsening ozone levels. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has delayed and rolled back requirements meant to hold companies accountable for their emissions.

As the public monitoring system has weakened, communities have increasingly turned to an alternative: low-cost sensors they can use themselves.

But a Floodlight investigation finds industry is moving to restrict that option, too.

Since 2024, lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky have passed strikingly similar bills — backed by chemical or manufacturing trade groups — that curb the use of community-collected data in enforcement actions.

The bills share a common thread: They block regulators from using air-quality data for enforcement purposes unless it meets EPA-approved standards. Similar bills in West Virginia have yet to pass.

In case after case, proponents have made the same argument: Community monitoring isn’t reliable enough for regulatory enforcement.

Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill designed to ensure accuracy, industry resisted.

The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” an official at the chemical giant Chemours wrote in an internal email.

An early-warning system in decline

Thousands of small, often-unremarkable instruments serve as the nation’s early-warning system for dangerous air — detecting pollution that people can’t always see or smell.

Some sit inside shelters the size of garden sheds. Others are mounted on rooftops or tucked into fenced compounds. Together, these monitors measure pollutants ranging from ozone and carbon monoxide to carcinogens such as benzene and vinyl chloride.

The network grew out of the 1963 Clean Air Act and transformed the way the nation tracked air pollution, giving regulators data they could use to identify dangerous conditions and hold polluters accountable. Since then, air pollution has fallen dramatically across much of the U.S.

But today, the network is “showing its age,” said Chet Wayland, who led EPA’s Air Quality Assessment Division for nearly two decades. “And it’s getting smaller over time.”

For example:

Leaks, termites, and ants plague monitoring stations in one state while officials in another have resorted to shopping on eBay for discontinued parts, according to a 2020 congressional watchdog report.

Adjusted for inflation, federal grants to support the network have fallen more than 35 percent over the past two decades, while the Trump administration tried unsuccessfully last year to eliminate them entirely — and is trying again this year.

The number of government air monitors nationwide fell by nearly half over the same 20-year period, according to EPA data.

The decline was especially pronounced among air monitors that track toxic chemicals, including those linked to cancer and other serious health effects.

For example, the network monitoring vinyl chloride — the carcinogen at the center of the 2023 train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio — shrank by more than half from 2004 to 2025. So did the network for chloroprene and benzene.

Floodlight analyzed the largest industrial sources of air pollution in Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio, and West Virginia — where the monitoring legislation was introduced — and compared what each one reported releasing against what public monitors in those states are capable of detecting.

For 71 of the 100 facilities examined, the chemical they release most isn’t measured by any government monitor in the state.

Hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, methanol — no air monitor currently reporting to the EPA measures those toxic chemicals.

Nelson Roque, an assistant professor at Penn State, co-authored a 2025 study that found nearly six in 10 U.S. counties have no public air monitor at all.

Such gaps matter most in communities already facing higher risks. Black and low-income people bear a disproportionate share of elevated cancer risks from air toxics, according to the EPA.

“We’ve realized the value of other infrastructure, and yet not this one,” Roque said. “Last I checked, we all breathe air.”

The shrinking public network has set the stage for another fight: who gets to measure the air, and whose data counts.

Louisiana: A monitoring gap, and the fight to keep it

Public air monitors in Louisiana — a national hub for oil, gas, and petrochemicals — are often located miles from major industrial polluters and fail to test for some of the most dangerous chemicals, a recent Floodlight investigation found.

Community groups have tried to fill that gap. A $500,000 grant awarded under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act would have allowed the Louisiana Environmental Action Network to establish air monitoring in 27 communities it identified as pollution hot spots.

But the group was able to install monitors in only four communities before the Trump administration canceled the grant last year.

“It’s like having your legs knocked out from under you,” said LEAN executive director Marylee Orr.

In 2024, meanwhile, Louisiana became the first state to restrict the use of community air monitoring data.

The Louisiana Chemistry Association helped draft the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act (CAMRA), which cites the need for “science-based standards” and bars the use of air pollution data in enforcement or regulatory actions unless it’s captured by EPA-approved monitors. That equipment typically costs tens of thousands of dollars.

In a previous statement to Floodlight, LCA president David Cresson defended the law, saying it ensures “data used to enforce our state’s environmental protection laws complies with minimum U.S. EPA standards” and doesn’t stop residents from monitoring air quality for their own information — only from using unregulated methods for enforcement purposes.

The same period brought other rollbacks, some sought by the chemical industry’s most powerful national lobbying group. The American Chemistry Council — the LCA’s national counterpart — spent more than $22 million lobbying in 2024, ranking 10th among 9,200 organizations tracked by an independent watchdog group.

The ACC and the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers last year requested a blanket two-year exemption from Biden-era regulations meant to cut certain toxic emissions by nearly 80 percent at roughly 200 chemical manufacturing plants. They didn’t get the blanket exemption — but individual plants that applied did.

So far, President Donald Trump’s EPA has granted more than 60 petrochemical facilities exemptions from the rule, and the agency is now weighing whether to rescind it entirely.

The ACC also successfully lobbied against federal rules that would have required about two dozen chemical plants to conduct fenceline monitoring for ethylene oxide, a carcinogen that contributes substantially to the elevated cancer risk in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley.

The national trade group did not respond to Floodlight’s questions about its lobbying or its involvement in Louisiana’s CAMRA law. Nor did it explain its role in promoting similar legislation in other states.

But in an emailed statement, the ACC said it has invested in community air-monitoring projects and “publicly advocated for expanded access to credible air quality information.” It said it supports monitoring that produces reliable, transparent data and gives communities and regulators information they can use to make informed decisions.

Kentucky takes a page from Louisiana

Odors from Rubbertown, an industrial complex that housed tire and synthetic rubber plants during World War II, have long bothered residents in west Louisville, Kentucky. So, in the early 2000s, the city’s Air Pollution Control District, the EPA and others launched a study that confirmed what residents had long known: The air had unacceptably high levels of toxic pollutants.

A plan was enacted, regulations were revised, and the air was continuously tested. More than 15 years later, regulators announced toxic air contaminants in the Louisville metro area were down by almost 80 percent — with the most dangerous chemicals cut by 96 percent.

Despite the success of expanded air monitoring in Louisville, Kentucky lawmakers have moved in the opposite direction. In March 2025, 10 months after Louisiana’s CAMRA law, they passed House Bill 137, which also restricted how air-monitoring data can be used in enforcement actions.

Lloyd “Rusty” Cress, executive director of the Kentucky Chemical Council, told the Kentucky Lantern that the bill was similar to Louisiana’s community air monitoring legislation. The law says air needs to be tested with “scientifically defensible” methods — echoing a phrase used in an ACC blog post in 2023.

The ACC, the American Petroleum Institute, Dow Chemical and Chemours all lobbied for it.

Jess Loizeaux, a Chemours spokesperson, said the company doesn’t object to community air monitoring. “We object to community air monitoring results being used for enforcement decisions without first verifying the validity and accuracy of the data through official tests performed by trained technicians at the appropriate regulatory authority,” she told Floodlight.

Kentucky’s political push unfolded against a backdrop of major gaps in public air monitoring. Only one of the state’s 25 largest air polluters is close to an air monitoring station that measures the top toxic chemical it emits.

Fewer than a quarter of the state’s counties have an air monitoring station.

Ohio’s restrictions meet with legal challenge

Ohio’s new air monitoring rule was tucked into last year’s budget bill with no named sponsor. It, too, stops regulators from acting on air-monitoring data collected by community groups.

“When we take away the ability for those folks to have a reasonably priced monitor … for their own protection, we’ve just taken any tool they had right out of their hands,” said Miranda Leppla, an attorney who sued the state over the new rules last year on behalf of environmental groups.

The lawsuit also challenges another provision in the budget bill that instructs state regulators to remove Ohio’s “air nuisance rule,” which allowed citizens to take legal action against companies whose emissions endanger public health.

One of the plaintiffs, Donna Ballinger, lives in Middletown, Ohio, hundreds of feet from a steel manufacturing plant that frequently rains down black, white, and gray particles onto her house and yard, she said. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car.

“My fear is cancer,” Ballinger told Floodlight.

She has an air monitor mounted in her front yard. But Ohio’s new requirement has made it impossible to use the data such monitors collect “as evidence of the nuisance conditions,” the lawsuit says.

The Ohio Chemistry Technology Council backed the measure. The group did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview.

Tony Long, general counsel for the Ohio Chamber of Commerce, said businesses are concerned that uncalibrated air monitors will spread misinformation.

“Given our litigious nature in this state, we think that the guardrails make sense,” he told Floodlight. “You don’t want to be stopped for speeding on an uncalibrated speed gun.”

With more than 90 public air monitoring stations, Ohio has a more robust air monitoring network than some states. Yet none of Ohio’s 25 largest air polluters are within 20 miles of a public air monitoring station that measures its top toxic emission. In fact, no air monitor in the U.S. measures the chemical that 10 of them release most.

Ohio’s Syensqo Specialty Polymers plant, which makes a resin used in plastics, released more than 130 tons of volatile organic compounds into the air last year, according to Ohio regulators.

The nearest air monitoring station is about 4 miles away — in West Virginia — and doesn’t measure VOCs.

Industry resistance stalls West Virginia efforts

West Virginia’s Department of Environmental Protection runs just 14 monitoring sites in 12 counties. The other 43 counties have no state monitoring stations at all.

None of West Virginia’s 25 largest air polluters has a public air monitor within 25 miles that measures the pollutant it releases most. For 17 of the facilities, no air monitor anywhere in the U.S. measures their top toxic emission.

In 2024, a state bill backed by the West Virginia Manufacturers Association would have barred community air monitoring data from use in regulation, enforcement and lawsuits; it passed the House but died in the Senate — partly because industry couldn’t agree on what to include.

A compromise version of the 2024 bill, drafted to address the concerns of some lawmakers, would have let regulators use community data if the monitors met manufacturer standards. Industry refused to support it.

In emailed comments about the compromise bill, West Virginia Manufacturers Association Bill Bissett said it “neuters” the measure and was “now toothless.” Chemours’ Jeff Fritz wrote, “I do not like this draft,” and said the bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” according to emails obtained by Mountain State Spotlight. Neither Bissett nor Fritz responded to requests for comment.

Subsequent bills, introduced in 2025 and 2026, also failed.

Why monitoring matters

Evidence shows that better monitoring can reduce pollution — and potentially save lives.

In 2018, the EPA made refineries begin monitoring benzene along their fencelines, and within five years, the number of refineries above EPA’s benzene action level dropped by half, according to a report by the Environmental Integrity Project.

While some states have made it difficult to know what’s in the air, others have been proactive:

California is funding equipment and training for residents in fenceline communities to monitor for things like pesticides, hexavalent chromium, and other toxic chemicals. From 2017 to 2025, the state budgeted $1.4 billion to help communities that have historically been overburdened with air pollution.

Colorado required four industrial plants to install fenceline monitors that measure hydrogen sulfide, benzene, and hydrogen cyanide in real time. The state also bought two mobile vans that regularly sample the same pollutants in surrounding neighborhoods.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and its contractors operate 33 automated gas chromatographs — sophisticated equipment that collects air samples every hour and provides near real-time readings of volatile organic compounds.

But in much of the U.S, those who live near industrial plants still have little way to know what they’re breathing.

An unanswered question

Reonda Victor lives in Louisiana’s heavily industrialized corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, where flares from industrial plants often illuminate the night sky.

Her mother, grandmother, and sister all had breast cancer. Concerned about her own risk, she underwent genetic testing, which showed no predisposition to the disease, she said.

The closest public air monitoring station to her home — which lies in an area where air pollution poses one of the highest cancer risks in the country — tests only for lead.

Did industrial pollution cause the illnesses that struck her family members? She can’t say. But proper air monitoring could help answer that question, she said.

“Without information, we don’t know.”

Kentucky Public Radio contributed to this investigation.

text:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday, September 13, 2026, witnessed the signing of a contract to establish a plant producing various types of electric batteries within the frame of a partnership between Egyptian battery maker BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer.

The contract was signed by Chairman of BME Maged Wahib and Luo Director of international investment at CATL Luo Haining, in the presence of Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem, MBA/PMP - Sr. IT Project Manager Amin Karim Ghabbour and BME board member Lotfy Tadros.

BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

The new plant aims to establish a specialized industrial base for battery systems in Egypt, initially producing batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, with plans to expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.

The project is intended to serve the growing transport and energy sectors and support manufacturing and exports.

The plant’s first phase will have an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour, with initial investments exceeding 2 billion Egyptian pounds (dlrs 39 million). The second phase will raise capacity to 5 gigawatt-hours annually and include production of passenger-car batteries as well as batteries for storing solar and wind energy.

The project targets a local component ratio of 40% and is expected to supply both domestic and international markets, while creating jobs and developing technical skills for Egypt’s workforce.

The partnership combines Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities with CATL’s battery technology, production equipment and technical support. The plant will supply locally manufactured battery systems to vehicle manufacturers in Egypt, reducing reliance on imports and associated shipping and logistics costs.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Madbouly welcomed the agreement with CATL, saying the company was one of the leading global players in the battery industry and had extensive expertise and capabilities.

He said the government expected work on the project to begin quickly and that it would take the necessary steps to support the development and localization of battery manufacturing in Egypt.

The minister of Industry said the plant represented an important step towards developing Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capacity as the global shift towards electric vehicles and energy-storage solutions accelerates.

Hashem said automotive component industries were a cornerstone of Egypt’s national program to develop the automotive industry and were key to attracting global carmakers.

He also said the agreement with the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer demonstrated the ability of Egypt’s industrial sector to meet international manufacturing requirements and produce competitive, high-quality products.

Project manager Amin Karim Ghabbour said the agreement was part of government efforts to deepen local manufacturing, localize modern industries and technologies and strengthen Egypt’s capabilities in producing automotive components, especially for electric vehicles and battery systems.

He said the partnership with CATL would combine advanced global battery technology with Egyptian industrial and engineering capabilities, supporting technology and knowledge transfer and the development of a local supply chain.

Ghabbour further added that BME aimed not only to produce battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles, but also to establish the foundations for an integrated battery industry that could eventually expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.

The expansion, he said, would create new opportunities for investment, manufacturing and exports and support Egypt’s efforts to become a regional hub for emerging industries.

text:
BME is a newly established joint venture founded by Egyptian private bus and truck maker Manufacturing Commercial Vehicles Company (MCV), Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies, a publicly traded company and solutions provider for Egypt’s automotive sector, and CATL.

CATL is a Chinese zero-carbon energy technology company and manufacturer of battery energy storage systems (BESS) for electric vehicles (EVs).

The project will have an initial production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) annually, rising to 5 GWh in the second phase. The second phase will include batteries for passenger vehicles and clean-energy storage batteries for solar and wind power applications, with a targeted local content rate of 40 percent. No timeline or location for the project has been disclosed.

The plant aims to establish a specialized industrial base for battery systems in Egypt, initially focusing on batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, with future expansion into passenger car batteries and energy storage solutions.

It will also expand Egypt’s manufacturing and export capabilities in the battery industry, support knowledge transfer, develop a local supply chain, and reduce shipping costs, reflecting the country’s ability to “meet global manufacturing standards and produce high-quality, competitive products,” Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said.

The project will also utilize Egypt’s location, production capabilities, and engineering expertise, combined with advanced Chinese technology, production equipment, and technical support. This will help meet local and global demand for electric batteries in the transport and energy sectors.

Egypt’s exports to China surged by around 200 percent year-on-year to $840.8 million in the first six months of 2026, up from $280.5 million in the same period in 2025. China is one of Egypt’s largest trading partners and a major source of FDI across multiple sectors, including construction, textiles, electronics, energy, transport, and manufacturing.

The two countries have been working to expand their economic partnership, with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s recent historic visit to Cairo resulting in the signing of multiple memorandums of understanding on industrial manufacturing, technological, economic, and supply-chain cooperation, as well as the launch of the third phase of the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone.

The project comes as Egypt’s trade deficit continues to widen, most recently by 58.5 percent year-on-year to $7.5 billion in June 2026, up from $4.7 billion in the same month a year earlier, amid ongoing regional tensions that have caused supply-chain disruptions and a higher import bill.

Furthermore, Egypt has been stepping up efforts to transform its assembly-based automotive industry into an integrated sector by manufacturing complete vehicle bodies domestically, alongside launching a vehicle replacement programme to boost demand for locally made cars and reduce steel imports, as the country’s automotive sector was rising steadily at the beginning of this year.

The automotive feeder industries are an important pillar of the National Automotive Industry Development Programme (AIDP) and a key driver of efforts to attract global automakers, Hashem said.

The AIDP was launched in October 2025 to localize vehicle manufacturing, attract international investment, boost exports, and reduce reliance on imported cars and components. It targets raising local value-added content to 60 percent, increasing the share of domestic industrial components to more than 35 percent, and reaching an annual production volume of 100,000 vehicles.

This aligns with the government’s strategy to improve industrial development and component usage as part of efforts to expand non-oil manufactured exports, improve the economy’s resilience to external shocks, and raise annual exports to $100 billion by 2030.

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

The artificial intelligence boom poses serious health risks while the Trump administration is dismantling crucial safeguards designed to protect the public, according to former officials at the federal agency responsible for environmental protection.

A report released Thursday by the Environmental Protection Network—an organization led by former Environmental Protection Agency staffers—outlines hazards from the rapid rise of data centers. Among those is pollution from increased power demand, which is linked to asthma, cancer, neurological harm and heart and lung disease.

The EPA’s stated mission is to protect human health and the environment. But under President Donald Trump and EPA administrator Lee Zeldin, the federal government has targeted pollution limits and safeguards, weakened enforcement of environmental rules, expanded fossil fuel power generation and moved to give the AI industry dangerous carveouts, experts warn.

“Our government and especially EPA should be making choices that protect people’s health, not choices that leave families carrying more pollution and more risk,” Marc Boom, senior director of public affairs at EPN and a former senior advisor at the EPA, said at a press briefing.

As data center electricity demand grows, the Trump administration is pushing fossil fuel energy over the development of cleaner options. The EPN report outlines 30 federal actions that it says increase pollution-related health risks, though the authors note it’s not an exhaustive list. The actions include extending the life of fossil fuel plants that were soon to be retired, expanding coal while loosening requirements for coal-ash cleanup, rolling back clean air rules and fast-tracking data-center permitting.

“Clean Air Act requirements don’t bend for industry, but they also should not be weaponized,” wrote EPA spokesperson Cora Mandy in an emailed statement. “In each action EPA has taken, the agency has returned regulations to the best reading [of] the Clean Air Act after years of overreach by previous administrations.”

Mandy added that one pillar of the Trump administration’s EPA agenda is to make America “the AI Capital of the World.”

Americans broadly oppose the rapid data center buildout, often citing rising utility bills, water demand, low job creation and localized noise and air pollution. A YouGov survey of registered voters conducted for EPN in April found that 84 percent thought Trump should be tougher on corporations that violate environmental laws and more than two-thirds were highly concerned about policies that fast-track data center projects.

“Data centers and the way that they’re not being regulated are threatening to take us back 200 years by building fossil fuel and polluting infrastructure right on top of where people live,” said Saul Levin, program director at the Center for Nonviolent Conflict Research and host of The Hum, a podcast about data center resistance.

Levin speaks with people opposing data centers across the country and said they often share health-related concerns.

READ: Falls Township Residents Say They Were Left in the Dark Throughout Data Center Planning Process

“When it comes to health, people just know that they’re being fed something that’s a bad deal in every way,” Levin said.

More pollution means more missed days of school and work, higher medical bills and more illness and death, the former federal workers wrote in the EPN report. They called on the EPA to put public health ahead of AI expansion by restoring and enforcing pollution safeguards.

“If America is going to undertake an industrial and energy buildout of this magnitude, we should not be taking away the environmental cops’ resources or restricting their ability to act—we should be strengthening the EPA’s ability to hold polluting facilities accountable,”said Larry Starfield, a former principal deputy assistant administrator in the EPA’s enforcement office.

“We still do not know the full health toll, and that should argue for more vigilance, not less.”— Dr. Lynn Goldman, former EPA assistant administrator

In a study from June, researchers at universities in California and New York found that under a high-growth scenario for the data center industry, its air pollution could contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma symptom cases, 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs in 2028.

That doesn’t account for recent federal rollbacks, noted Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former EPA assistant administrator.

“These alarming numbers may capture only part of the picture,” Goldman said. “We still do not know the full health toll, and that should argue for more vigilance, not less.”

READ: Montour County Residents Prove Community Organizing Can Defeat Data Centers and Halt Corporate Land and Power Grabs

Although much of the health fallout from policy decisions today will unfold over decades, Goldman noted that some will be immediate, like impacts on pregnant people and fetal development, or heart attacks caused by excessive particulate matter pollution.

“Some of the health impacts from air pollution that are the worst impacts play out in real time,” Goldman said. “It does not take years and years to see an increase in death from that kind of pollution.”

text:
Australia-Based A1 Lithium Plans Emery County, Utah, Production Operations

Critical minerals company A1 Lithium Inc. plans to establish operations in Emery County, Utah. The $569 million project is expected to create 138 jobs.

The investment will include the construction of a new lithium carbonate production facility located in Utah’s Paradox Basin, which will produce high-purity, battery-grade lithium carbonate for the U.S. electric vehicle and energy storage markets.

“Apart from the advantageous geological conditions of the Green River Lithium Project, A1 Lithium decided to invest in Utah due to the high-level support for the development of critical mineral projects to meet the strategic objective of re-establishing supply chains in the USA,” said Anson Resources President Bruce Richardson. “Utah’s transparent mining policies and aim of making quick application determinations were also a factor in this decision. We have received an unprecedented level of support from GOED and UIPA as well as other Government of Utah agencies for which we express our appreciation. We are excited to proceed with this project that we expect will bring about a generational change in the economy and livelihood of the people of Green River and south-eastern Utah.”

To support the project, the Utah Governor’s Office of Economic Development (GOED) awarded A1 Lithium a post-performance tax reduction through the state’s Rural Economic Development Tax Increment Financing program. The Utah Inland Port Authority (UIPA) board also approved an incentive for the project.

“Developing domestic supply chains for critical minerals is a key focus of both state and national energy infrastructure strategies,” noted GOED Commissioner Jefferson Moss. “The Green River Lithium project in Emery County marks a significant advancement for rural economic growth in Utah. It establishes a sustainable and long-term industrial base, creating well-paying jobs in rural areas and strengthening Utah’s role in producing energy materials domestically.”

A1 Lithium Inc. is the U.S. subsidiary of Australia-based Anson Resources, a critical minerals company focused on developing lithium resources. The company specializes in lithium brine development and direct lithium extraction, with plans to produce high-purity, battery-grade lithium carbonate for electric vehicles, energy storage, and other advanced technology markets.

“A1 Lithium’s investment in south-eastern Utah will be transformational for the City of Green River, Utah’s production of critical minerals, and our nation’s broader reindustrialization efforts,” added EDCUtah Executive Director Ryan Starks. “EDCUtah is proud to support A1 Lithium as they grow and expand, and our network looks forward to continuing to support the company as they invest in the region and create long-term opportunities.”

“UIPA is helping Green River translate private investment into long-term economic capacity,” said UIPA Executive Director Ben Hart. “This post-performance incentive aligns A1 Lithium’s growth with regional priorities and ties public support directly to actual investment and job creation.”

text:
A Quinnipiac University poll of Pennsylvania voters this summer found that 74% say they would oppose building an AI data center in their community, while 16% would support it, with 10% not offering an opinion. This compares to Quinnipiac’s February poll, when 68% said they would oppose an AI data center in their community and 20% would favor it, with 12% not offering an opinion.

Guardrails on PA data centers

Governor Josh Shapiro in August issued an executive order demanding that data center developers meet energy affordability, community engagement, economic development and environmental protection standards. If they don’t, he said, the commonwealth will not give them permits to build and operate.

Click to resize

PA data center permit tracker

In correlation with the governor’s executive order, Pennsylvania’s Department of Environmental Protection has created a “data center permit tracker.” You can check it out online.

Community solar update

Community solar projects are legal and operating in 44 states. But Pennsylvania — heavily influenced by the fossil fuel industry — is not one of them. A bill that would make community solar legal here has passed the state House of Representatives. Its fate now rests in the Republican-controlled Senate where it is mired in committee. Community solar allows renters and others who can’t put solar panels on their roofs to invest in a local solar array. The energy generated by the array is sold to the electric grid and the proceeds typically knock five-to-20% off an individual investor’s home electric bill.

Energy recommendations

PennFuture, an environmental advocacy group, in August produced recommendations for Pennsylvania’s energy future. They include: (1) requiring 35% of electricity to be generated by renewable energy sources; (2) passing Community Solar enabling legislation; (3) Incentivizing solar development on rooftops of warehouses, fulfillment centers, and large government buildings; and (4) promoting sustainable economic development by leveraging environmental standards attached to financial resources.

PA lawmakers rated on conservation

Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania has created a “scorecard” showing how state legislators voted on key bills impacting the environment in the last two years. The 2025-26 Pennsylvania Environmental Scorecard gives each member of the legislature a score on their environmental voting. Just enter your address and you can see the score for the lawmakers that represent you in Harrisburg.

Changing national forest rules

The U.S. Department of Agriculture plans to end a 25-year-old rule limiting road building and logging on 44 million acres of national forest land. That includes the half-million acre Allegheny National Forest in Pennsylvania. The Forest Service will accept, until midnight Sept. 21, public comments before a final decision is made. To comment, go to Regulations.gov. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule currently protects 25,000 acres in Pennsylvania from logging, mining and other destructive human activities, according to PennEnvironment.

Clean energy second-quarter growth

Clean energy investments in the U.S. surged in April, May and June reaching the second-largest quarterly investment in history just behind the third quarter of 2025 when people were hurrying to buy EVs before tax credits ended. That’s according to the Rhodium and MIT Clean Investment Monitor. Nearly all of the increase came from retail sales of rooftop solar and home battery storage systems.

text:
Public has right to know what data centers are doing

I am writing regarding the Environmental Protection Agency’s recent actions to gut pollution controls for artificial intelligence data centers.

Modern AI data centers can use enormous amounts of electricity, as much as a city in one location. Local grids struggle to keep up with such demands. EPA’s efforts to deal with this problem come at the expense of clean air and the public’s right to know what is happening in their community.

Specifically, the Trump administration allows construction to begin before obtaining air permits; AI data centers to run their dirty generators more frequently; certain power plants to not install any pollution controls for acid rain; and companies to seek and receive “minor source” air permits without gathering public input.

Limiting the transparency and accountability of the buildout of these dirty data centers will have real consequences. Large-scale generators at AI data centers are usually powered by diesel, polluting the air we breathe with dangerous chemicals. The public deserves clean air and has a right to know what kind of pollution data centers are pumping into our communities. It's your right to know.

Marcia Schulz, Silver Lake

People with disabilities at risk as services are cut

I’m angered by the Department of Justice’s recent memo authorizing states to institutionalize more people with disabilities. This means removing people from society and shutting them into nursing homes, psychiatric hospitals, segregated schools and sheltered workshops, rather than funding community- or home-based care which offer more autonomy, undoing decades of law and Supreme Court precedent. SinceOlmstead v. L.C., in 1999, states have been required to support disabled people in the most integrated setting. Institutionalization is supposed to be the last resort.

Sadly, states have already started slashing disability services because of Donald Trump’s Medicaid cuts. The budget’s advocates professed that safety-net programs for the “most vulnerable Americans,” would be safeguarded, but children and people with disabilities have been hit hardest.

The DOJ’s memo is part of the administration’s sweeping series of changes impacting how disabled people learn, live, work and otherwise interact with society. For example, the Education Department’s responsibilities for special education and civil rights have been reassigned to the Department of Health and Human Services, raising concerns about whether children will continue to have access to free, appropriate public education. We must resist this and every attempt to make America’s most vulnerable invisible.

Charlotte Onderick, Stow

Blessed to ride with March on Washington activists

I had the great benefit of grabbing a seat on a bus with the Urban League to attend the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington and Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. Though I don’t know anyone who’s ever enjoyed the physical trip to D.C. on a bus itself, due to its unavoidable, uncomfortable nature, I consider the experience to have been a gift of a lifetime.

What made the trip special were all of the young Americans, the UAW members from all over Ohio supporting Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton, and, most of all (for me) was the chance to relax and talk with a few dozen members of the marvelous Delta Sigma Theta Sorority from all over the country.

These proud women and avowed social activists are part of a historic sorority that was born in 1913, and had, as their earliest dedicated mission, the women’s suffrage movement. Their wisdom, accomplishments and kindness to an old guy like me from Cuyahoga Falls reminded me that a day on a bus with almost no sleep was meaningless in comparison to the blessings I received in return.

Todd Schneider, Cuyahoga Falls

Remembering what the rubber workers stood for

I do hope it does not offend anyone, when I say: It’s about time.

The rubber industry of Akron has been reported on, in glowing terms in the recent past. As well it may, but a key component, labor, has nearly been completely overlooked. Just why did the workers resort to various kinds of disruptive behavior? Because they were really Communists? They just wanted to tear down the thing of beauty that had been created by General, Goodyear, Firestone and Continental? Absolutely not.

Their employers were using them as they used all other factors of production. Buy an input and use it up, as cheaply as possible. Their living expenses were paid for by trading their skills and labor for their weekly paycheck. The workers were simply looking for an equitable trade in the process.

As has happened to some degree throughout history, when people find that they are in need or hurting they band together for the common good. The United Rubber Workers resulted.

Also, please note that while Akron has enjoyed the URW as an International Union, it is not the only one. Please do not overlook the International Chemical Workers Union that originated in about 1937, about two years after the United Rubber Workers Union. It is still located in the Mitchell Building on West Market Street. (The ICWU is now a part of the United Food and Commercial Workers Union, UFCW, while the URW is now a part of the United Steel Workers Union).

Philip Kroll, Akron

The state of things under Donald Trump

So Dear Leader Don wants to rename New Mexico (we won't even mention Lake Ontario), but why stop there? Just be done with it and rename the states Trump 2 through 51. You might ask why not 1 through 50? Well … we all know who Number 1 is, don't we?

Once Trump is gone, the new president can create CURDS (Commission to Undo Really Dumb Stuff).

Chris Walker, Fairlawn

Akron needs more rules for more people

The city of Akron and the mayor keep coming up with new rules for the police to follow. It has to be tough for the police to think of so many rules in the heat of the moment.

Maybe the mayor and the city should come up with rules for the criminals. This way the criminals would have to think more about committing their crimes.

Gary Flower, Akron

description:
Concerns over Gulf fish farms are wide-ranging, from nutrient pollution due to excess food and fish waste to the potential for escape.
Manna Fish Farms, a New York-based company, is proposing to install 12 to 14 net pens more than 20 miles off Pensacola.
It would be the first such commercial fish farm in U.S. federal waters, said Manna Fish Farms CEO Donna Lanzetta.
He notes, however, that a true commercial fish farm would have to be far, far larger.

text:
The redfish were biting out in the Gulf, but not in the way they’re usually caught.

Instead, about 1,000 of them in total, all around 10 inches long, were in an artificial pen enclosed by netting, a machine on the surface tossing out tiny food pellets every five minutes.

Ashley McDonald, the scientist managing what is currently the only finfish farm in the Gulf’s open waters, stood atop a yellow platform surrounding the wind-swept pen, waves lapping against its sides. She reflected on the small-scale but compelling aquaculture experiment.

“We can grow fish because we have funding to do it,” she said. “Does that mean that that’s actually economically viable?”

It is a question rooted in a rising moment of peril for the Gulf, and it holds high-stakes consequences for Louisiana and the rest of the states along its shores.

The floating aquaculture platform operated by the Dauphin Island Sea Lab off the coast of Alabama is scientific in nature, designed to shed light on whether such small projects can be ecologically and economically sound. But it may offer a glimpse of the future.

A warming climate, overfishing, economic opportunities and Americans’ voracious appetite for seafood are building momentum for large-scale fish farming in the Gulf of Mexico, which President Donald Trump has renamed the Gulf of America.

It would mark a monumental shift in the country’s commercial fishing industry, as well as for a water body more known for its oil rigs, barrier islands and beaches. For supporters, it is a way to reduce the huge number of imported seafood consumed by Americans, currently around 85% of the total by some counts.

But industrial-scale Gulf aquaculture is intensely controversial, with serious environmental considerations, the risk of hurricanes and concerns from traditional commercial fishermen, including Louisiana’s struggling shrimpers.

Some large-scale aquaculture operations in other countries have led to escaped fish, the spread of disease, the misuse of antibiotics and harmful pollution, among other problems. Those pushing for fish farms in the Gulf say such problems have been accounted for and overcome in their plans, while noting the strict requirements for federal permits and related regulations.

Are large fish farms a necessary and inevitable means of adapting? Or a recipe for disaster? That debate is raging — and the eventual outcome is no longer a far-off possibility.

Another demonstration project in the Gulf, in federal waters off Sarasota, Florida, was recently granted final permits and hopes to be in the water early next year, with a plan to grow up to 20,000 redfish, which are officially known as red drum. That project is a pilot and far smaller than what would be needed for a true commercial operation, but its aim is to help open the path to large-scale fish farms.

A far larger proposal for a commercial-scale fish farm off Pensacola is pending as the plans advance through the country’s byzantine permitting process. And separately, the federal government has identified three areas off Texas as potential sites for aquaculture.

Louisiana has much at stake. The state is still the nation’s second-leading seafood supplier behind Alaska, with an annual economic impact of more than $2.4 billion, despite its rapidly declining wetlands habitat, according to state data.

At the same time, future conditions may only worsen. One recent study projected that increased drought related to climate change could periodically lead to big decreases in Gulf catch.

“I do see aquaculture as being one of the top solutions to the need for proteins for humans. It’s surprisingly hard to do it right,” said Benjamin Kirtman, dean of the University of Miami’s Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science and a co-author of the study.

“You want to make sure you do it in such a way that you don't disrupt the rest of the ecosystem. All of that takes an enormous amount of time.”

‘What I liked about the fish business’

Harlon Pearce’s love of the outdoors is obvious from a look around his office, where mounted bass and deer heads adorn the walls. But seafood is also his business, as it has been for more than 60 years.

His career straddles the industry’s rugged past and the rapidly shifting currents of today.

Below him are the cavernous warehouses for Harlon’s LA Fish, where workers were busy on a recent day slicing filets from slimy mounds of whiskered catfish. Pearce, 80, still shows up at 4:30 a.m. to prepare for deliveries to his plant in Kenner, not far from Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport.

While attending Loyola Law School, he decided he enjoyed the seafood business more than being a lawyer. Early on, he worked for legendary seafood dealer Preston Battistella, whose business had its roots in the heyday of New Orleans’ French Market, before starting his own company.

“I didn't like law, didn't like the reading,” Pearce said.

“I didn't like having to go back to somebody's case to tell me what I could and couldn't do. What I liked about the fish business is I could make a difference and make a change, because nothing was written in stone.”

He recalls the bonanza days, when commercial fishing for redfish was still legal and gill nets were allowed for speckled trout, helping New Orleans build its reputation as a culinary cornucopia. That all changed in the 1980s and beyond as population declines for those species and others became apparent.

Pearce laments the state of the business now. He largely blames commercial fishing regulations, which he calls too restrictive, though recreational anglers and fisheries biologists would certainly disagree.

While still dealing largely in local seafood, Pearce has adapted to include purchases of imports and out-of-state product. His main local supplies include catfish, sheepshead, black drum, shrimp, crab and oysters.

He laments that prices for certain types of wild-caught, local seafood have spiked while regulations have put popular species out of reach for commercial fleets.

It is partly for that reason that Pearce is not opposed to aquaculture in the Gulf. He feels that it would offer a lifeline to the industry if done responsibly. He calls it absurd that New Orleans restaurants serve redfish farmed in ponds in other states, mainly Texas.

“If we don't have the production that we need, to do what we need to do, we're dead,” he said. “So anything that helps us get production, and especially in a moderately priced way, I'm all for. I don’t care what it is.”

But where Pearce sees a lifeline, others sense a potential catastrophe.

Concerns over Gulf fish farms are wide-ranging, from nutrient pollution due to excess food and fish waste to the potential for escape. To make them economically viable, they would necessarily have to be large-scale, and opponents note the Gulf already suffers from an annual "dead zone" created by nutrient pollution flowing down the Mississippi River.

Manna Fish Farms, a New York-based company, is proposing to install 12 to 14 net pens more than 20 miles off Pensacola. Each one would be capable of holding 500,000 pounds of fish, but the company intends to stock them at half their capacity, or 250,000 pounds, to avoid overcrowding.

Each net pen would be 9,000 cubic meters, or the volume of about three and a half Olympic-sized swimming pools. The initial plan is to grow redfish there, and the pens could be submerged 40 feet below the water’s surface.

It would be the first such commercial fish farm in U.S. federal waters, said Manna Fish Farms CEO Donna Lanzetta.

Acy Cooper, president of the Louisiana Shrimp Association, said local shrimpers have been fighting the prospect of offshore aquaculture for years. Even small-scale farms are unacceptable to him, he said.

“That right there is the beginning of the end,” said Cooper, whose organization still has around 500 members despite the local shrimping industry facing numerous challenges. “If it starts, you’re never going to stop it.”

For environmental organizations like Healthy Gulf, concerns are similar. Healthy Gulf was among the groups that filed suit to try to stop the experimental project now set to move forward off Sarasota.

Christian Wagley, a coastal organizer with Healthy Gulf, noted the loss of habitat for wild fish, ranging from the disappearing marsh of Louisiana to the dying seagrasses and oyster beds in other areas of the Gulf Coast. He said the country should focus on restoring that habitat and supporting traditional commercial fishermen instead of pushing for fish farms.

“There will never be one fish farm only in the Gulf, and they'll never be small, because you have to have the economies of scale,” said Wagley. “And so I think for them to make it profitable, they would have to have literally miles and miles of industrial-scale fish farms.”

‘Producing more of this ourselves’

The emerging industry, however, argues the main concerns involving large-scale aquaculture will be overcome through water quality monitoring, careful food management and secure pens, among other measures. They appear to have an ally in the current administration.

Trump, in his first term, signed an executive order on “promoting American seafood competitiveness” that in part aimed to ease the highly complex permitting process for aquaculture.

There is also support in Congress, where a bill known as the MARA Act has been introduced aiming to establish a framework for sustainable offshore aquaculture.

More recently, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration identified 13 “Aquaculture Opportunity Areas” as holding potential for fish farms. They included 10 off California and three in the Gulf off Texas.

Three areas of Louisiana had been identified as potential sites earlier in the process, but those were later removed amid objections from commercial fishing organizations and environmental groups.

Even so, the areas that did make the cut are largely symbolic. Aquaculture development in the Gulf is by no means limited there, and that is beginning to be made emphatically clear.

After an eight-year permitting process, Hawaii-based company Ocean Era recently received the final green light for a pilot demonstration project around 40 miles off Sarasota, Florida.

The so-called Velella Epsilon project will grow up to 20,000 redfish in a net pen measuring 55 feet in diameter and about 23 feet deep. Like the Dauphin Island experiment, its nets are designed to be strong enough to resist sharks, and the entire structure can be submerged in the case of storms.

Neil Sims, Ocean Era’s CEO, hopes the project can be in the water early next year. The company has run two similar pilots off Hawaii.

It wanted to start with a smaller project “that wasn't going to scare anybody in terms of its scale, its potential impact, and allow the Gulf fishing and boating community to see for themselves what offshore aquaculture actually looks like,” said Sims.

He notes, however, that a true commercial fish farm would have to be far, far larger. The pilot off Florida is only about 1% of what would be needed, said Sims.

But Sims is an unapologetic evangelist for the industry. He believes the country has no choice, and he contends that monitoring has demonstrated that if you put the pens in deep enough water, far enough offshore, there is no significant impact on the surrounding ecosystem.

He points to what labels itself the country’s only commercial fish farm operating in the open ocean, run by Blue Ocean Mariculture and producing 900 tons of kanpachi per year in state waters off Hawaii. Sims helped found what later became Blue Ocean.

“It's a great way for us to start to produce the seafood that we need,” said Sims, mentioning the large amount currently imported.

“We need to be producing more of this ourselves, and we need to be creating jobs and building an industry here.”

There are numerous onshore or coastal aquaculture farms, including in Louisiana, growing everything from catfish to oysters. But onshore aquaculture does not carry the same risks to the surrounding ecosystem as open water finfish farms.

Not all environmental groups oppose open ocean aquaculture. But they stress that it must be done responsibly, and with utmost caution.

‘Grow great things’

The small “AquaFort” fish farm off Alabama’s coast comes into view like a sturdy raft floating atop the Gulf’s waters, black piping and a yellow platform framing its perimeter. In a reminder of the Gulf’s industrial legacy, a hulking gas rig looms in the far-off distance.

The Dauphin Island Sea Lab, in partnership with other institutions, won a federal grant for up to three years to operate it, and it is modeled after a similar project off New Hampshire. The scientists overseeing it are hoping to find out if it can be sustainable and ecologically sound, potentially providing traditional commercial fishermen with the option of operating their own for a supplemental source of income.

The platform is actually moored to the seafloor, and it is surrounded by netting to keep the redfish in and predators out. It is part of a dual system of protection that initially included copper mesh, but that will soon be changed to a lighter plastic version.

It is divided into two pens, each one 20 feet by 20 feet, at a depth of 12 feet. The feeder that tosses out pellets for the redfish is solar-powered, and an underwater camera system allows the scientists to monitor the fish remotely.

Cages along the sides hold oysters and algae being grown alongside the fish. The idea is that the oysters can filter the water, and the algae can absorb the excess nutrients being produced by the fish.

Part of the experiment involves whether those, too, can be harvested and marketed, though the current location does not allow for the oysters to be sold.

In June, the scientists returned with commercial fishermen to harvest the redfish. Afterward, they distributed them to seafood markets for free this time and collected feedback.

They would have to be labeled as farmed, but would allow Alabamans a chance to buy redfish from the Gulf.

Like Louisiana, Alabama bans commercial fishing for the species, whose numbers plummeted by the 1980s, though they are farmed in ponds, particularly in Texas.

It will all be a test to gauge interest in the idea — and, potentially, an entirely new industry. McDonald sees the smaller-scale projects like her own as holding potential for wide acceptance.

“We can grow great things in the Gulf. They're local, they're right here, we know how they're grown, we know where they came from,” she said.

“You're able to actually kind of promote and show people that this is Gulf seafood. This didn't come from Indonesia or South America.”

title: Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky pass industry-backed bills blocking community air data in ...
description:
New laws in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky, however, limit how much that locally gathered information can matter in requests for regulatory enforcement, according to Floodlight.
Here's what to know Lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky started enacting closely aligned bills in 2024 with support from chemical and manufacturing trade associations.
Questions about who can document pollution — and what regulators can do with that evidence — reach beyond Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky.
• In Kentucky, lawmakers advanced limits on air pollution penalties for self-reporting polluters in 2024.
Community health protections hinge on air monitoring and on whether governments are willing to act when pollution is found.
text:
Residents near factories sometimes rely on inexpensive air sensors of their own when official monitors are too few or not close enough to major industrial facilities.

New laws in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky, however, limit how much that locally gathered information can matter in requests for regulatory enforcement, according to Floodlight.

Here's what to know

Lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky started enacting closely aligned bills in 2024 with support from chemical and manufacturing trade associations.

Under those measures, enforcement cases cannot be based on air readings unless they come from monitors built to EPA-approved standards, devices that can run into the tens of thousands of dollars.

West Virginia has seen similar proposals, but none have been enacted.

Federal grants for the system have dropped by more than 35%, after adjusting for inflation, and the number of government air monitors across the country has been cut by nearly half. That reduction formed the backdrop for these new laws.

Monitoring for toxic pollutants has thinned even further, with networks measuring vinyl chloride, chloroprene, and benzene each declining by more than half from 2004 to 2025.

Chet Wayland, a former longtime leader of the EPA's Air Quality Assessment Division, acknowledged that the network was "showing its age" and "getting smaller over time," Floodlight reported.

Nearly 60% of U.S. counties have no public air monitor at all, according to a 2025 study co-authored by Penn State assistant professor Nelson Roque.

More background

The people most affected are often those already living alongside major industrial operations.

Floodlight found that 71 of the 100 largest industrial polluters it reviewed across Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio, and West Virginia released, as their top chemical, a substance no government air monitor in that state measures.

Kentucky approved House Bill 137 in March 2025, after Louisiana passed the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act, and Ohio adopted a comparable limit through its budget bill.

Under Kentucky's law, air testing must use "scientifically defensible" methods.

"When we take away the ability for those folks to have a reasonably priced monitor … for their own protection, we've just taken any tool they had right out of their hands," said Miranda Leppla, a lawyer who sued Ohio over its new rule on behalf of environmental groups, per Floodlight.

Donna Ballinger, who lives near a steel plant in Middletown, Ohio, told Floodlight what she worried about most.

"My fear is cancer," she admitted.

What's being done?

The Environmental Integrity Project says that once the EPA required refineries in 2018 to track benzene at their fencelines, the number above the agency's benzene action level fell by half within five years.

In California, residents of fenceline communities have received funding for monitoring equipment and training, and the state set aside $1.4 billion between 2017 and 2025 for communities that have long carried heavy pollution burdens.

Colorado now requires four industrial plants to conduct real-time fenceline monitoring.

In Texas, the Commission on Environmental Quality and its contractors run 33 automated gas chromatographs that deliver near-real-time measurements of volatile organic compounds.

A court challenge is pending against Ohio's law, while community organizations in places including Louisiana continue pressing for stronger local air data despite funding setbacks.

Reonda Victor, in Louisiana's industrial corridor, told Floodlight, "Without information, we don't know."

Where can I learn more?

Questions about who can document pollution — and what regulators can do with that evidence — reach beyond Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky.

Elsewhere, lawmakers and major companies are also trying to shape when air violations lead to penalties and when enforcement gets tougher.

• In Kentucky, lawmakers advanced limits on air pollution penalties for self-reporting polluters in 2024.

• In Detroit, Stellantis pursued a workaround to avoid state particulate emissions rules the same year.

• In Delaware last year, lawmakers approved major restrictions for big corporations by expanding pollution fines.

Community health protections hinge on air monitoring and on whether governments are willing to act when pollution is found.
