There are now 17 EV assembly plants operating in Ethiopia, with the government targeting 60 by 2030.
The question for Africa specifically is no longer whether Chinese EV companies will sell vehicles there.
Africa must negotiate the industrial value The arrival of Chinese EV manufacturing shouldn't be judged only by the number of factories or assembly plants announced.
FAQ Which African countries are central to Chinese EV manufacturing in 2026?
text:
Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers are no longer treating overseas markets simply as destinations for exports. They're increasingly moving production closer to consumers, and Africa is beginning to appear on that manufacturing map.

A 2026 map of selected major Chinese EV production facilities outside China shows the scale of this shift. The facilities span Europe, Central Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia, and Africa now has a genuine cluster of its own: Egypt, Kenya, South Africa, and increasingly Ethiopia, with Chery appearing across three of the four markets.

The pattern signals a real change in strategy. Instead of shipping finished vehicles from China into every market, manufacturers are increasingly combining imports with local assembly and manufacturing, reducing logistics costs, responding to local industrial policy, and securing access to regional markets they'd otherwise only reach as an exporter.

The timing matters too. In the first half of 2026, China exported 5.096 million vehicles, up 65.3% year on year, with new energy vehicles contributing over 46% of that total. Chinese passenger vehicle exports rose 77.5% year on year in August alone, even as domestic sales declined 23.7%. That's a domestic market under real pressure pushing capital and capacity outward at speed, and Africa is one of the destinations absorbing it.

South Africa: the industrial anchor

South Africa represents the most significant single industrial move so far. Chery officially inaugurated its Rosslyn manufacturing plant in Pretoria in July 2026 after acquiring the former Nissan facility, with production beginning mid-2027, an initial run of 15,000 vehicles planned for the second half of that year, on a line capable of producing gasoline, hybrid and pure electric models. Chery is retaining 692 existing employees and targeting up to 3,000 additional jobs across manufacturing, supply chains and related services.

South Africa carries an advantage most African markets can't easily reproduce: a mature automotive manufacturing industry, established component suppliers, technical skills, ports, and decades of experience producing vehicles for export, backed by an industrial policy framework built specifically to attract manufacturers and increase local content. That's what makes the Rosslyn acquisition more significant than the arrival of another Chinese brand, it places an established manufacturer directly inside one of Africa's most developed automotive production corridors, with Chery signalling the plant will support exports, R&D and broader regional operations.

Kenya: assembly as an industrial foothold

Kenya's opportunity is less about large-scale vehicle manufacturing and more about using assembly to build an industrial foothold, leveraging its access to the East African market and an established commercial vehicle sector. Chery has announced plans for local CKD assembly through its Kenyan partner Caetano Kenya, with industry sources reporting a separate $20 million Chery-related investment targeting 5,000-6,000 vehicles annually. Dongfeng is separately partnering with Kenya's ePureMotion to begin local EV assembly in 2026, using Associated Vehicle Assemblers facilities to cut costs and improve competitiveness, alongside a KSh1.4 billion Global Motors Centre investment assembling Jetour vehicles in Mombasa.

The strategic question for Kenya is whether these facilities remain simple assembly operations or become the foundation for a wider local supply chain, since that distinction determines the actual economic value the country captures from the investment.

Egypt: the cluster model

Egypt is becoming the most concentrated Chinese automotive manufacturing location on the African map, drawing on a large domestic population, a location bridging North Africa, the Middle East and international shipping routes, available industrial zone capacity, and government policy increasingly focused on domestic automotive production.

SAIC's MG brand anchors this cluster. Al Mansour Automotive is developing a $135 million manufacturing facility with first-phase capacity of 50,000 vehicles annually, expanding to 100,000 units, targeting more than 45% local components, a meaningfully higher bar than simple final assembly. The more consequential possibility is what happens when several manufacturers converge in the same industrial geography: component suppliers, logistics companies, technical training institutions and maintenance businesses can develop around them collectively, potentially creating an actual automotive production base rather than isolated assembly plants.

Ethiopia: the most aggressive policy bet

Ethiopia has taken a different and, in some respects, more radical route than any of the other three markets: it has banned the production, import and assembly of fossil-fuel-powered cars outright, making itself, in the words of one Chinese automaker's local partner, "an ideal market for reputable companies" with nowhere else for demand to go but electric.

The results are already visible at scale. There are now 17 EV assembly plants operating in Ethiopia, with the government targeting 60 by 2030. Guangzhou Automobile Group (GAC) has introduced its EV models to the Ethiopian market through its partner Huajian Group, which will sell vehicles, build charging infrastructure, and initiate local assembly operations, while GAC's country leadership has said the company will move into EV production directly to tap the market's scale. Ethiopia's government has been explicit about its ambition: officials describe the country as positioned to become an automotive manufacturing and assembly hub for Africa, citing abundant hydropower energy resources, a young trainable workforce, access to the African Continental Free Trade Area, and investment incentives including free or leased land for EV after-sales investors.

The caveats are real, though, and worth stating plainly. Ethiopia's manufacturing sector contributed less than 7% of GDP as of 2023, constrained by a difficult regulatory environment and high cost of capital, and the country's own vehicle base is tiny relative to its population, only 1.7 million vehicles for 130 million people. Analysts covering the sector note the domestic market is likely too small yet for full-scale manufacturing plants on the Rosslyn or MG scale; the value Ethiopia is capturing right now is concentrated in assembly rather than deep manufacturing. But assembly at 17 plants and rising is still a genuine value-add relative to pure imports, and Ethiopia is also investing directly in the workforce behind it, partnering with Chinese vocational training experts to build local technician and educator capacity specifically for EV maintenance, manufacturing and repair.

The map shows a much bigger strategy

Africa becomes easier to understand viewed alongside the rest of the map. BYD already operates a 150,000-vehicle annual capacity plant in Thailand covering stamping, welding, painting, final assembly and component production. In Europe, BYD is preparing to begin production at its Szeged plant in Hungary in Q4 2026, manufacturing inside the EU rather than depending on vehicles shipped from China, an increasingly important consideration as Europe imposes trade measures on Chinese EVs. The same logic shows up in Turkey, Spain, Uzbekistan, Malaysia and Indonesia.

The geography isn't random. Chinese manufacturers are placing production capacity in markets where local manufacturing improves their competitive position, whether that's tariff avoidance, cost structure, or market access. The question for Africa specifically is no longer whether Chinese EV companies will sell vehicles there. They already do, across dozens of markets. It's whether Africa captures a meaningful share of the manufacturing, component production, servicing and technology transfer that comes with the next phase.

Why Africa is attractive right now

Chinese automakers face a genuinely difficult combination of circumstances at home and abroad: an intensely competitive, weakening domestic market, and increasingly restrictive trade policy in Europe and North America toward Chinese EVs specifically. Africa offers a different proposition: low vehicle ownership relative to population, rapidly growing cities, large unmet demand for affordable mobility, and cost structures that differ meaningfully from mature automotive markets. Small EV adoption today doesn't preclude a large addressable market over the coming decade, and Ethiopia's fossil-fuel ban shows how quickly a government can accelerate that addressable market by policy fiat rather than waiting for organic adoption.

Local assembly also changes the underlying economics directly. A vehicle assembled in Kenya, Egypt, South Africa or Ethiopia can qualify for different fiscal treatment than a fully built imported one, while manufacturers cut shipping costs and shorten supply chains. For governments, the appeal is equally direct: an imported vehicle generates taxes and sales activity, but a manufacturing plant generates employment, supplier contracts, technical skills, industrial infrastructure and eventually exports.

Africa must negotiate the industrial value

The arrival of Chinese EV manufacturing shouldn't be judged only by the number of factories or assembly plants announced. The more useful measure is how much value stays inside the African economy. A plant importing batteries, motors, electronics and body panels while performing only final assembly creates a fundamentally different economic impact than one progressively developing local suppliers, and that distinction is exactly what African industrial policy needs to be built around: clear local content targets, supplier development programmes, technical training, predictable tax treatment, and policies that encourage battery manufacturing, power electronics, charging equipment and vehicle software alongside assembly itself.

Ethiopia's vocational training partnerships and Egypt's 45% local content target are both, in different ways, attempts to get ahead of exactly this problem before it sets in. Without that kind of deliberate policy, Africa risks becoming the final destination for another generation of imported technology rather than a genuine participant in producing it.

The EV race is becoming a manufacturing race

The 2026 map captures a real shift in the global automotive industry. Chinese companies are building production capacity outside China precisely as their domestic market comes under pressure and trade barriers rise in some of the world's richest markets, and Africa, across four distinct models, South Africa's industrial anchor, Kenya's assembly foothold, Egypt's cluster strategy, and Ethiopia's policy-forced acceleration, is increasingly part of that calculation.

The first phase was bringing Chinese vehicles to African consumers. The second phase is building the vehicles closer to them. For all four markets, the immediate challenge is converting current investment into deeper industrial capacity rather than letting it settle at final assembly. For the rest of the continent, the question is whether these investments remain isolated national projects or become the beginning of genuine regional automotive supply chains.

The Uchumi360 insight

China is exporting more than electric cars. It's exporting the factories that will decide who captures the next generation of automotive value. South Africa is betting on industrial depth it already has. Kenya is betting on assembly as a stepping stone. Egypt is betting on cluster density. Ethiopia is betting on policy forcing the market's hand faster than any of the others. None of these bets has resolved yet, and that's precisely why the map is worth watching rather than treating as settled.

FAQ

Which African countries are central to Chinese EV manufacturing in 2026? Egypt, Kenya, South Africa and Ethiopia, each pursuing a different model, industrial anchor, assembly foothold, cluster strategy, and policy-forced acceleration respectively.

Which Chinese automaker has the broadest African presence? Chery, with facilities or planned facilities in South Africa, Kenya and Egypt.

What makes Ethiopia's approach different? Ethiopia has banned fossil-fuel vehicle imports and assembly outright, forcing EV adoption by policy rather than waiting for market demand, and already has 17 EV assembly plants with a 2030 target of 60.

Why is South Africa important to Chinese automakers? It already has an established automotive manufacturing industry, supplier base, skilled workforce and export infrastructure; Chery's acquisition of the former Nissan Rosslyn plant gives it a ready-made industrial base for African expansion.

Why is Egypt attracting Chinese automotive investment? A large domestic market combined with a strategic location linking Africa, the Middle East and international shipping routes, backed by government policy encouraging local manufacturing and a 45%+ local content target.

text:
President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report. They are urging — perhaps futilely — the president to adopt a “Data Center Health Protection Pledge” to signal that the administration is taking the environmental threat seriously.

At the start of his term, Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, proclaimed his goal of making America “the AI capital of the world” through deregulation. Since then, Zeldin and the White House have rolled back dozens of rules on top of cutting staff and funding at the US EPA.

As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape.

“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA.”

“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA,” Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and a former EPA assistant administrator, said at the briefing. “Instead, EPA is doing just the opposite, thinking first about industry’s needs and weakening or reconsidering limits on toxic chemicals and harmful pollutants.”

Goldman and other former EPA employees who are part of an independent organization called the Environmental Protection Network released a report this week that identifies 30 different federal actions since January 2025 that they say exacerbate health risks stemming from data center pollution.

That includes executive actions and proposals meant to curtail renewable energy projects while softening pollution regulations and exempting existing power plants and factories from certain standards. Of the 30 policy changes included in the report, 17 specifically mention AI or target data centers.

Trump released an “AI Action Plan” in July 2025, recommending “streamlining or reducing regulations” under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Superfund law to expedite permitting for data center projects and chip factories. “What the AI plan is really about [is] using unprecedented emergency powers to grant massive new exemptions for data centers and specifically fossil fuel infrastructure,” Tyson Slocum, energy program director at the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, told The Verge at the time.

Trump has essentially laid the policy groundwork for new gas projects to power energy-hungry data centers, ranging from turbines installed on-site to power plants built specifically to serve tech companies. Meanwhile, demand for advanced chips needed for generative AI is reviving the production of forever chemicals that don’t break down easily and build up in the environment and human bodies. All this new infrastructure can spread pollution far from the data centers they support.

“You do not need to be near a data center to be affected, because the pollution doesn’t just come from the data centers themselves,“ Goldman says.

“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now.”

Last year, hundreds of current EPA employees fired off a public letter addressed to Zeldin saying, “EPA under your leadership will not protect communities from hazardous chemicals and unsafe drinking water, but instead will increase risks to public health and safety.”

The new report cites a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology that found that air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028. The toll could be even larger after factoring in the policy changes outlined in EPN’s report, according to the organization. The US can avoid those losses by restoring clean air and water standards, as well as rebuilding federal agencies’ capacity to enforce those rules, the EPA alumni argue.

“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, EPN’s senior director of public affairs, said in the briefing. “EPA should be measuring how this buildout is changing pollution, who is being exposed, what it means for their health, and making all of that information public. That is what a Data Center Health Protection Pledge should mean in practice.”

Responding to the report in an email to The Verge, EPA spokesperson Cora Mandy said, “In each action EPA has taken, the agency has returned regulations to the best reading [of] the Clean Air Act after years of overreach by previous administrations.” She also reiterated the agency’s commitment to “Protect Human Health and The Environment” while simultaneously prioritizing “Making America the AI Capital of the World.”

text:
Massachusetts is putting fresh funding behind the clean energy workforce, pairing job training with marine science as offshore wind development continues to grow along the East Coast.

In all, the $4.2 million package is intended to help residents move into maritime and offshore wind careers while also funding studies tied to wildlife, fisheries, and ocean conditions.

Here's what to know

Announced last week by Gov. Maura Healey and the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center, the funding is being routed through two MassCEC programs. According to a press release, about $1.7 million of the funding is allocated to the Offshore Wind Works program and about $2.4 million to the Offshore Wind Science, Research, and Analysis program.

Rather than focusing only on construction, Massachusetts is investing in the people who will fill offshore wind and maritime roles and the research needed to guide the rapidly expanding industries.

On the workforce side, that includes training opportunities that can make it easier for residents to enter the field. Meanwhile, the marine research funding is meant to explore how the buildout may impact ocean ecosystems and commercial fisheries.

More background

Offshore wind has become one of the most closely watched parts of the clean energy economy, sitting at the crossroads of electricity, manufacturing, shipping, and coastal employment. For states such as Massachusetts, it creates an opportunity to build a supply chain close to home.

Training programs can help people qualify for steady work in construction, vessel operations, logistics, and maintenance without needing to leave the state. A stronger local workforce may also help projects avoid some of the labor bottlenecks that can drive up costs.

Expanding offshore wind is intended to add more clean electricity to the grid, which can help diversify power supplies and reduce dependence on the polluting fossil fuels that are also vulnerable to price swings. If projects are built more efficiently, that can affect the delivered cost of power that ultimately appears on electric bills.

Meanwhile, the Offshore Wind Science, Research, and Analysis funding supports the study of wildlife, fisheries, and the marine environment. It could help communities, policymakers, and developers make better, evidence-backed decisions.

Where can I learn more?

Massachusetts' latest funding announcement is part of a much bigger offshore wind rollout. These stories show how job training, project design, policy, and funding are shaping the industry:

• Hexicon is testing wind and fishing coexistence as offshore projects push into working waters.

• The U.S. Department of Energy is opening offshore wind career paths beyond traditional energy jobs.

• Federal backing for ocean and river turbines shows marine energy investment extending beyond wind.

These stories also help explain why Massachusetts is funding job training alongside marine research. Offshore wind tends to move more smoothly when workers, technology, and community concerns are all considered as part of the same plan.

authors: Nik Miles, TestMiles.com, Nik Miles, TestMiles.com

Hyundai Wants Mobility Business Beyond Car Sales The Waymo agreement fits a broader message Hyundai executives delivered in Seoul.
For Waymo, Hyundai offers an established global manufacturer with a U.S. plant and a fast-charging electric crossover that was designed for passengers rather than as a science project.
It is preparing to put factory-built vehicles into the supply chain of the largest commercial autonomous ride-hailing operation in the United States.
text:
(TestMiles) – Hyundai’s Georgia-built IONIQ 5 is moving from family EV to commercial robotaxi as Waymo prepares for a larger driverless fleet.

Hyundai spent years trying to persuade American families to buy electric vehicles. Its next customer may order them by the fleet and remove the driver.

At Hyundai Motor Company’s 2026 CEO Investor Day in Seoul, the automaker said deliveries of IONIQ 5 vehicles to Waymo are scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. The vehicles are intended to support Waymo’s expanding autonomous ride-hailing operation after integration with the company’s sixth-generation Waymo Driver.

The announcement advances a partnership first disclosed in October 2024. It also gives Hyundai a role in the commercial robotaxi market without requiring the automaker to build every piece of the service itself. Hyundai supplies the electric vehicle and manufacturing scale. Waymo supplies the autonomous-driving system and operates the passenger network.

The arrangement could become an important test of whether robotaxis can move beyond small, specialized fleets and become a repeatable automotive business.

The IONIQ 5 Becomes a Commercial Platform

The Waymo vehicle begins with an IONIQ 5, but it is not simply a showroom model with sensors attached after delivery. Hyundai says the autonomous-ready version includes redundant hardware and power-operated doors. The vehicles are assembled at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia before Waymo’s technology is integrated.

Redundancy matters because an automated vehicle cannot rely on a passenger to take over when a component fails. A commercial robotaxi also faces a harsher routine than most privately owned cars: long operating hours, frequent passenger stops, repeated charging and limited tolerance for downtime.

That helps explain the choice of the IONIQ 5. Its spacious cabin can accommodate passengers and luggage, while its 800-volt electrical architecture supports rapid DC charging under suitable conditions. Faster charging does not make the vehicle autonomous, but it can improve fleet utilization by reducing the time a revenue-producing vehicle sits at a charger.

Hyundai and Waymo originally said they expected to build the vehicles in significant volume over multiple years. They have not publicly provided a binding fleet total in the Investor Day material. That distinction is important because reported targets and corporate discussions are not the same as a confirmed production order.

Waymo Still Has to Validate the New Vehicle

Waymo began operating IONIQ 5 vehicles autonomously with a specialist present in 2026. That phase is part of adapting the company’s driving system to a new platform before fully driverless passenger operations.

Changing the vehicle underneath an automated-driving system is not trivial. Sensor placement, braking behavior, steering response, electrical systems, cabin controls and emergency procedures all have to work as one package. A system that performs well in one vehicle cannot be assumed to behave identically in another without extensive validation.

The federal government describes the type of operation used by commercial robotaxis as Level 4 high automation when the system performs the complete driving task within a limited operating area. That differs sharply from the driver-assistance systems sold to ordinary consumers, which still require a human to supervise the road.

Hyundai’s announcement is therefore a production milestone, not proof that the IONIQ 5 has completed every step required for unrestricted passenger service. Waymo will determine when its Hyundai vehicles are ready to carry riders without an autonomous specialist, and local operating approvals will continue to matter.

The distinction has become more visible as Tesla, Zoox, Waymo and other companies pursue different vehicle designs and regulatory strategies. Hyundai’s approach is comparatively conservative: retain the recognizable proportions and basic architecture of a conventional vehicle, then engineer it for an autonomous system with the necessary backups.

Hyundai Wants Mobility Business Beyond Car Sales

The Waymo agreement fits a broader message Hyundai executives delivered in Seoul. President and CEO José Muñoz said the group intends to become a “physical AI company” capable of producing and deploying robots and robotaxis. That strategy links conventional vehicle manufacturing with autonomous software, artificial intelligence and fleet services.

Muñoz also described robotaxis as part of Hyundai’s future in Japan. During a question-and-answer session, he explained that Hyundai had entered the Japanese market with battery-electric vehicles led by the IONIQ 5.

“And then Japan is part of that But precisely because Japan is so special, we want to be special in Japan as well. And we decided to enter the market only with the BEV technology, with the Ioniq 5. And then we want to bring the best mobility services also by bringing robotaxis and maybe others,” Muñoz said.

His spoken wording has been reproduced directly from the Investor Day transcript without quietly polishing the quotation.

Muñoz did not announce a Japanese robotaxi launch date or identify an operating partner for that market. That makes the American Waymo program the more concrete near-term development. Hyundai has a named partner, a specified vehicle, a Georgia production location and a delivery window. Japan remains an expression of direction rather than a scheduled commercial rollout.

For Hyundai, the business case extends beyond the number of vehicles delivered this year. Supplying autonomous fleets could create recurring high-volume demand, expose its vehicles to extreme real-world use and give the company experience engineering platforms for multiple autonomous-driving providers.

For Waymo, Hyundai offers an established global manufacturer with a U.S. plant and a fast-charging electric crossover that was designed for passengers rather than as a science project. That could make adding vehicles easier as the service enters more cities.

The unresolved questions are substantial. Neither company has disclosed the price of the fleet vehicles, their expected service life, the cost of converting them or when riders will first receive fully autonomous trips in a Hyundai. Regulators and communities will also judge the system by its safety record rather than the pedigree of the vehicle beneath it.

Still, the fourth-quarter delivery target marks a significant transition. Hyundai is no longer discussing robotaxis only as a future possibility. It is preparing to put factory-built vehicles into the supply chain of the largest commercial autonomous ride-hailing operation in the United States.

The next measure will not be how impressive the IONIQ 5 looks covered in sensors. It will be whether Hyundai and Waymo can manufacture, validate, charge, maintain and operate enough of them to make driverless transportation work reliably every day.

text:
source: Louisiana Illuminator

Former Environmental Protection Agency officials are warning that the Trump administration is dismantling pollution safeguards to accelerate construction of AI data centers, putting public health at risk.

The Verge reported this week that a group of EPA alumni released a new report on the issue and held a briefing urging the administration to adopt a voluntary commitment they are calling a Data Center Health Protection Pledge.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin set the direction early in the term, announcing a goal of making the United States what he described as the AI capital of the world through deregulation.

Since then, the agency has cut staff and funding while rolling back dozens of environmental rules.

What EPA Is Changing

Axios reported that the EPA is weighing a rule that would reclassify some temporary gas turbines as mobile rather than stationary equipment. That shift would make them significantly easier to permit.

John Walke, director of the Natural Resources Defense Council's federal clean air program, told Axios the agency was moving with unusual urgency, and that senior EPA officials had confirmed the effort was driven specifically by data center demand.

Three other regulatory changes are already in motion: a proposal to eliminate federal minimum requirements for public participation in permits covering smaller pollution sources; a separate rule proposed in May that would allow more construction to begin at data center sites before permits are secured; and guidance issued this summer telling power plants they may expand capacity to serve data centers under eased conditions.

Michele Nellenbach, whose role was not further specified in the sources, told Axios that building infrastructure faster and maintaining strong environmental safeguards are not mutually exclusive goals.

A Weakened Monitoring System

The rollbacks arrive as the nation's air-quality monitoring network is itself shrinking.

A Floodlight investigation, published via the LA Illuminator, found that federal funding for public air monitors has dropped more than 35 percent over two decades when adjusted for inflation, and that the number of government monitors nationwide fell by nearly half over the same period.

Much of the remaining equipment is aging.

Chet Wayland, who led the EPA's Air Quality Assessment Division for close to two decades, told Floodlight the network is aging and contracting.

Communities have turned to low-cost sensors as an alternative, but Floodlight found that lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky have passed legislation backed by chemical and manufacturing trade groups that blocks regulators from using community-collected data in enforcement actions unless it meets EPA-approved standards.

Community Opposition Grows

Anxiety about data centers is also mounting at the local level. Yahoo News reported that roughly 100 residents gathered at a church in Hanford, California, in late August to oppose a proposed facility at the county fairgrounds.

Hanford Mayor Mark Kairis told the Los Angeles Times the issue had moved from a national concern to a state and now a local one, and that feelings were running high.

One attendee, Darian Orduno, told the Times she was worried about what pollution from a data center could do to her newborn son's lungs, and that the issue would shape how she votes in the midterms.

State Assembly candidate Esmeralda Villegas told the gathering that technological progress should not come at the expense of the communities where these facilities are built.

The EPA did not respond to requests for comment from Axios beyond referring reporters to a January regulatory filing.

title: A federal court says the government can lie to you. That will backfire - Salon.com
description:
The government can let you be poisoned and lie about it, and you’re just supposed to suck it up?
What we learned is that the city knew it,” Lt. James Brosi, president of New York City’s Uniformed Fire Officers Association, told CNN.
But arguing about a constitutional right to clean air and water — something as far down on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs as it gets — is just bonkers.
In countries including Uruguay and South Africa, a right to clean water is enshrined in their constitutions.

text:
A week ago, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed a lawsuit against Jackson, Mississippi, which alleged that the city knowingly let residents drink lead-contaminated water, violating their right to bodily integrity and accurate information from the government. Kurt Engelhardt, a judge appointed by President Donald Trump, thumbed his nose at that reasoning, ruling “The Constitution does not provide redress for every governmental wrongdoing.” He added, “These deprivations, while grievous, do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right.”

A lot has happened in the past week, from assaults on voting rights to a lot of arguing about different maps to the president apparently offering $5,000 bribes to voters. But this ruling should get a lot more attention, especially Engelhardt’s bit about there being no “constitutional right to truthful information from officials during a public health crisis.”

Is that really where we’re at as a society? The government can let you be poisoned and lie about it, and you’re just supposed to suck it up? This issue is deeply related to the newly released trove of documents that indicate that New Yorkers were “misled” — essentially lied to — about air quality risks following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The 170,000 documents, released by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani ahead of the tragedy’s 25th anniversary, detail how the public was repeatedly reassured that the air near the collapsed towers was safe. But that wasn’t the case, and those exposed are now at elevated risks of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, not to mention cancer.

“We were dying with every breath we took down there. What we learned is that the city knew it,” Lt. James Brosi, president of New York City’s Uniformed Fire Officers Association, told CNN. This is even more alarming in light of reporting this week from The Washington Post that “The number of 9/11 survivors who are receiving aid for cancer has roughly tripled over the last five years.”

Start your day with essential news from Salon.

Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The ruins at Ground Zero were certainly a public health crisis. But according to Engelhardt, it doesn’t matter that the Environmental Protection Agency told New Yorkers not to worry and breathe it all in. This makes you wonder what the “protection” part of their agency is actually about, but it does make it more apparent why Mamdani’s opponents are attacking him over 9/11. For the easily distracted, it’s great deflection from their own failures to protect Americans.

The bottom line is this: It’s absurd that we are even having this discussion in 2026. Ideally, we should be debating whether internet access or education are human rights. I’m more on the fence about that than healthcare or free speech, which are undeniable human rights in my opinion. But arguing about a constitutional right to clean air and water — something as far down on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs as it gets — is just bonkers.

This isn’t true everywhere. As Mother Jones reports, “in at least nine US states, and in more than a dozen other countries, clean drinking water is in fact a protected right. In countries including Uruguay and South Africa, a right to clean water is enshrined in their constitutions. New York’s constitution, as of a 2021 amendment, states that “each person shall have a right to clean air and water, and a healthful environment.” So too in Massachusetts, where “the right to clean air and water’ has been constitutionally protected since 1972.” Maybe that sucks for Mississippi, but let’s not overlook the institutional-racism aspect of this either. Again from Mother Jones: “Jackson is more than 80 percent Black and has a poverty rate that is more than double the national average.” It’s not hard to read between the lines here.

Engelhardt may be technically correct that there’s no explicit law on the books about bodily integrity, but he’s wrong in a much broader sense. If government doesn’t have a responsibility to provide safe access to air and water — and doesn’t even have to tell the truth about it — then what is even the point of the government in the first place? People in judicial positions, like Engelhardt, seem unaware that chipping away at the very foundations of functional society like this threatens to make it unable to function — and that people won’t tolerate being poisoned or lied to like this forever. The backlash could be severe.

Maybe it’s difficult for the government to tell the truth and enforce some basic standards of public health. The alternative, though, is to ensure its own destruction.

text:
BRICS leaders on September 12 adopted a Terms of Reference and Action Plan for the BRICS Photovoltaic Industry Working Group and called for “value addition and economic diversification” in resource-rich countries as part of a wider push to strengthen clean technology manufacturing and resilient supply chains across the Global South.

The measures were part of the 45-page New Delhi Declaration adopted on the first day of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, which brought together the bloc’s 11 members. The expanded grouping, which also includes 10 partner countries, represents 49.5 per cent of the world’s population, 40 per cent of global Gross Domestic Product and 26 per cent of global trade.

The declaration also advances cooperation on low-emission hydrogen, smart grids, energy storage, sustainable mobility and climate finance, while linking energy transition with industrial development and economic resilience.

Solar manufacturing gets new BRICS framework

Under the photovoltaic industry action plan, BRICS members will establish national knowledge portals and support a BRICS Solar Photovoltaic Cooperation Roadmap covering technology, finance and skills.

The proposed roadmap provides an important opportunity to translate this scale into deeper industrial cooperation, according to Subrahmanyam Pulipaka, CEO, National Solar Energy Federation of India. “By bringing together the manufacturing strengths, technological capabilities, and rapidly growing markets of BRICS+ along with lessons from India’s solar success, we have an opportunity to make solar technologies more affordable, accessible and scalable.”

The declaration also calls for greater developing-country participation in higher-value manufacturing through investment, technology transfer and industrial cooperation and advances the BRICS Global Value Chain Action Plan 2026-2030.

“The bloc appears to be organising around competitiveness and forwarding a shared agenda in clean technology manufacturing for the Global South,” said Trishant Dev, deputy programme manager, Climate Change and Green Economy Programme, at Centre for Science and Environment (CSE).

The declaration also calls for fair competition in renewable energy markets and links clean technology manufacturing with efforts to make supply chains more resilient.

Critical minerals linked to economic diversification

On critical minerals, BRICS leaders affirmed their commitment to “reliable, responsible, diversified, resilient, fair, sustainable, and just supply chains”, while linking mineral development to domestic value addition, economic diversification and sovereign control over resources.

The declaration calls for greater participation by developing countries in higher-value manufacturing through investment, technology transfer and industrial cooperation.

Jagjeet Sareen, head of Asia-Pacific, Dalberg Advisors and host of the Bharat Climate Forum, said the affirmation on critical minerals, solar, green hydrogen and other clean technologies complemented the push for diversified manufacturing and clean-energy-based electrification.

“The affirmation by BRICS leaders on the need to promote reliable, responsible, diversified, resilient, fair, sustainable, and just supply chains of critical minerals, solar, green hydrogen and other clean tech is greatly valued, as it complements the push for diversified manufacturing and clean energy-based electrification across countries,” he said.

Energy security remains central to transition

The declaration calls for “just, orderly, equitable, and inclusive energy transitions”, while foregrounding diversified energy sources and resilient value chains. It states that fossil fuels “will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies”, reiterating the bloc’s emphasis on energy security alongside the transition.

“BRICS nations comprise a diverse mix of developing and emerging countries with growing energy needs, industrialisation aspirations, and multiple development challenges. It is unlikely that we will hear a fossil fuel phaseout declaration any time soon,” said Avantika Goswami, programme manager, Climate Change and Green Economy Programme, CSE.

“However, BRICS’ rapidly growing adoption of clean technologies like solar energy and electric vehicles positions them well to aim higher and aspire for a faster transition rather than lock-in vast amounts of fossil fuel infrastructure. BRICS nations are already generating more than half of the world’s solar power. Doubling down on scaling up renewable energy and economy-wide decarbonisation is the need of the hour, not only to cut emissions, but also to shield from volatility and supply disruptions like those precipitated by the Hormuz crisis,” she added.

The declaration also links the conflict in West Asia to energy and supply chain security, calling for the protection of civilians and critical infrastructure and the maintenance of trade, supply chains and energy flows. It links energy security with national security and development, while calling for stable energy supplies and protection of critical energy infrastructure alongside emissions reductions and equitable energy transitions.

As part of its focus on the energy transition, the declaration welcomes the BRICS Guiding Principles on Smart Grids and Energy Storage and India’s proposed BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage. Members also welcomed ongoing work on interoperable standards for zero and low emissions hydrogen and a joint report on hydrogen value chains.

Climate finance and debt constraints

The declaration identifies high debt burdens as a constraint on development and climate spending and calls for coordinated international action to improve debt sustainability and expand governments’ fiscal space.

It welcomes a central-bank report on sustainable and green finance, including adaptation, examining financing gaps and ways to make climate projects more bankable. It also calls on developed countries to provide “additional, adequate, predictable and accessible” finance, technology and capacity support for adaptation in developing countries.

BRICS also records progress on its Multilateral Guarantees initiative, including technical work and pilot transactions aimed at improving creditworthiness and reducing financing costs for development projects. The New Development Bank is expected to expand resource mobilisation and local-currency lending.

Ulka Kelkar, executive director, climate, economics & finance, World Resources Institute India, said the proposed BRICS Insurance Resilience Centre and BRICS Risk Lab could facilitate cross-country disaster risk pooling.

“BRICS countries are already large donors of climate finance, not just recipients, and the New Development Bank can continue to support projects for sustainable development and climate adaptation,” she said.

Mobility and resilient infrastructure

The declaration announces a BRICS Urban Mobility Hub for cooperation on accessible, affordable and smart urban transport, along with a BRICS Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework and continued discussions on a proposed BRICS Railway Research Network.

Members also committed to promoting Sustainable Aviation Fuels and Low-Carbon Aviation Fuels to reduce emissions from international aviation.

The declaration further backs early-warning systems and voluntary principles for climate-resilient urban infrastructure, while recognising the role of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure in technical assistance, policy and financing.

Global South seeks greater role in institutions

The declaration calls for greater representation of developing countries in global institutions, including changes to International Monetary Fund voting shares and World Bank shareholding to reflect their growing economic weight.

It also seeks more representative and transparent selection of IMF and World Bank leadership, greater developing-country representation in the United Nations Security Council and senior UN positions, and increased participation by women.

Manjeev Puri, distinguished fellow at The Energy and Resources Institute, said the declaration reaffirmed key positions of the Global South and called for greater cooperation on cross-border trade and payments.

“The BRICS has reiterated some of the most important positions of the Global South,” he said. “We’ve strongly called out against unilateralism.”

Rathin Roy, distinguished professor, Kautilya School of Public Policy and Economic Advisor and Dean, GITAM School of Humanities and Social Sciences, noted that the term “Net Zero” is absent from the declaration.

He said the document frames sustainable development more broadly, with climate change presented as part of a wider set of issues including environmental degradation and inequality.

India’s year-long chairship convened more than 400 meetings and engagements across 30 cities in 2026. China will take over the BRICS chairship in 2027 and host the 19th BRICS Summit.

title: US bans on Chinese EVs could shield automakers, leave consumers missing 'Toyota moment'
description:

text:
A growing debate over U.S. restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles goes beyond trade policy.

Critics say the crackdown could protect domestic automakers in the short term while giving American drivers a raw deal.

Here's what to know

Gilbert Smith of CarBuzz argued that U.S. limits on Chinese EVs, including a 100% tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles and restrictions tied to connected-car software and hardware, may do more to shield automakers than to protect workers or consumers.

Smith framed the comparison through an earlier shift in the U.S. auto market, which he branded as the "Toyota moment." The company entered the country in 1957 but managed only 287 sales by the end of 1958. Later, its small, efficient cars become more appealing as gasoline rose from about 37 cents a gallon in 1971 to 57 cents in 1975.

The account highlighted the 1975 Corolla's advertised highway rating of 42 miles per gallon. Smith said Toyota sold 283,909 vehicles in the United States that year, enough to beat Volkswagen by 16,191 and take the top import spot.

He argued that Chinese EV companies such as BYD and Geely could create similar competitive pressure by pushing U.S. automakers to build better, less expensive electric cars. Without that pressure, families may face higher prices, slower innovation, and fewer chances to lower what they spend on gas.

Cleaner, more affordable EVs can reduce tailpipe pollution in neighborhoods while helping households keep more of the money they would otherwise spend on fuel.

More background

Smith said the official reason for the connected-car restrictions is national security, especially the concern that Chinese companies could collect American data.

Broad worries about data collection do not fully explain why Chinese vehicles are being singled out. He noted that Microsoft, Facebook, Twitter, and smartphone companies all feature tracking methods and data collection, which supports the view that the restrictions may be more of an industrial safeguard.

While the United Auto Workers union says Chinese automakers benefit from heavy support from the Chinese government, Smith contrasted that with the $80 billion bailouts for America's biggest car companies in the late 2000s.

To show that demand already exists, Smith said farmworkers in rural Texas buy Chinese trucks in Mexico, including the BYD Shark, and bring them across the border for legal use on private land.

Smith also pointed to Chinese battery progress, including one that boasts 745 miles on a single charge and solid-state technology. He argued that excluding Chinese companies from the U.S. market could leave American communities waiting longer for low-cost, low-pollution transportation.

What's being done?

American companies aren't standing still, per Smith. Factorial Energy, a U.S.-based battery company, is working with Stellantis to stay competitive in next-generation battery development.

Automakers, meanwhile, could respond the way competitors have in earlier eras by building compelling vehicles that meet what shoppers want on price, range, and efficiency.

More EV competition could mean more affordable models, lower fueling expenses, and cleaner air in the communities where people live and work.

If the U.S. wants a transportation future that is cheaper, cleaner, and more competitive, giving incumbents protection may delay the market pressure that produces better cars for everyone.

Where can I learn more?

The argument over Chinese EV restrictions spills into software rules, battery supply chains, and the race to keep up in the global auto market. Those policies can shape which technologies make it to U.S. drivers, how fast automakers respond, and what buyers end up paying.

• In the United States, Chinese software rules could cut automakers off from global EV markets.

• U.S. battery makers still face risks of import dependence on Chinese minerals for energy storage.

What happens with Chinese EV imports may help decide who sets the pace for the next era of carmaking. For drivers, that could shape which cleaner, low-cost technologies arrive first and how long they take to get here.

title: Government Clown Just Can't Quit Coal Power - CleanTechnica
description:
By Friday afternoon, Wright was right back at it again, forcing yet another emergency order on yet another coal power plant.
One Coal Power Plant Closes… The J.H.
Campbell coal power plant in Michigan was the subject of the Friday morning decision.
Back in 2022, the Energy Department surmised that hundreds of former coal power plants could host nuclear energy facilities.
Who Needs Coal Power?
text:
The arc of justice bent around and kicked US Energy Secretary Chris Wright in the shins Friday morning, when a federal court ruled that he can’t make up “emergency” orders to save old coal power plants from the dustbin of history. However, the ruling only applied to one power plant. By Friday afternoon, Wright was right back at it again, forcing yet another emergency order on yet another coal power plant. Break out the popcorn, there’s gonna be a fight!

One Coal Power Plant Closes…

The J.H. Campbell coal power plant in Michigan was the subject of the Friday morning decision. In May of 2025, Wright began issuing a series of “emergency” orders forcing the plant to stay open. The first order came down just days before the plant was set to close, marking the final stage of a years-long planning effort involving multiple stakeholders including the facility’s owner, Consumers Energy (see more J.H. Campbell background here).

The Sierra Club is among the organizations challenging the Campbell orders and other similar orders in multiple states. As noted by Sierra Club and its partners, a normal Energy Secretary only issues emergency order on request, in consultation with the relevant stakeholders, and only under extreme conditions such as weather or wartime.

Wright, in contrast, has been sprinkling emergency orders around willy-nilly like that lady in the park throwing breadcrumbs at pigeons, and the U.S. Court for the District of Columbia finally called him on it.

“The section of the Federal Power Act that allows emergency orders ‘is essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop,'” PBS reported, citing the decision written by Appeals Court Judge Cornelia Pillard for the three-judge panel, in a unanimous finding that reversed Wright’s emergency order. Judge Pillard further noted the emergency order disrupted a “long and carefully planned retirement.”

“Use of emergency authority “‘is triggered only when there is a need for immediate, essentially last-resort action and the circumstances require action by DOE in particular, as opposed to action by the state or states responsible for resource adequacy,'” PBS further reported, again citing Pillard.

…Another One Opens!

As if to spit in Judge Pillard’s eye, Secretary Wright promptly clapped back with another emergency order just hours after the District Court released its ruling.

“U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright today issued an emergency order to keep affordable, reliable, and secure coal generation in the State of Washington online to help address critical grid reliability issues facing the Northwestern region of the United States,” the Energy Department wrote on September 11.

“The emergency order directs TransAlta Centralia Generation, LLC (TransAlta) to ensure that Unit 2 of the Centralia Generating Station in Centralia, Washington, a coal-fired power plant, remains available to operate,” DOE elaborated.

As noted by DOE, Centralia Unit 2 was originally scheduled for retirement at the end of 2025. Wright issued the first emergency order on December 16, just days before it was set to retire.

Break Out The Popcorn!

Somewhat hilariously, the Centralia order will not prevent the site from being converted to support wind, solar, or energy storage operations. That’s because the carefully planned closure of Unit 2 was carefully planned around replacing coal with natural gas, not renewables, at least until the 2040’s.

That’s not going to sit very well with whatever natural gas distributor was banking on a new revenue stream supplying Unit 2. Nuclear energy stakeholders may be feeling a bit peckish as well. Back in 2022, the Energy Department surmised that hundreds of former coal power plants could host nuclear energy facilities.

Readers, if you have any insights into that angle, drop a note in the discussion thread. Meanwhile, to make matters even more hilarious, it turns out that Unit 2 has been off-grid ever since last December, despite Wright’s whackadoodle emergency orders.

“In December 2025, TransAlta announced an agreement with Puget Sound Energy to transition the remaining generating unit to natural gas, delivering up to 723 megawatts of power when needed,” the Washington State Department of Ecology explains.

“However, that same month, the U.S. Department of Energy issued an emergency order requiring TransAlta to keep the Centralia plant operational as a coal power plant,” WSDE adds.

“Despite the emergency order, which has since been extended twice, the plant has not actually been called on to supply electricity to the grid since mid-December,” the agency adds again, by way of reminding everyone that the very careful planning process leading up to the scheduled closure of Unit 2 involved ensuring that other power generation resources were ready and waiting.

Who Needs Coal Power?

The Centralia debacle is just one example of Wright’s inane — and expensive — efforts to keep an aging, creaking, outdated form of power generation cranking away well into the 21st century.

On Friday afternoon, the leading environmental law organization Earthjustice emailed an explainer to interested parties (including CleanTechnica), explaining exactly why there is no emergency where Wright pretends one exists.

The J.H. Campbell plant is a regional facility located within the territory of MISO, the Mid-Continent Independent System Operator responsible for keeping the kilowatts flowing among states in the midsection of the US.

“The regional grid, MISO, had unused available excess generation far exceeding the amount of power supplied by the coal plants under ’emergency’ 202(c) orders during Winter Storm Fern, during this summer’s hottest days, and last years’ hottest days” Earthjustice summarizes.

“On June 23, the grid’s most stressed period during the summer [of 2025], MISO had a surplus of unused excess resources of 7,941 MW. Meanwhile, according to EPA data, Campbell was providing a maximum of 760 MW. Thus, MISO had a surplus of unused excess resources more than 10 times larger than the amount of power being provided by Campbell,” Earthjustice elaborates.

Similarly, Earthjustice found that during the most stressed period during the winter of 2025-26, MISO enjoyed “a surplus of unused excess resources of at least 5,000 MW to 7,500 MW.”

They Do Maths

That’s just a snippet from Earthjustice’s much longer, detailed analysis. Meanwhile, Wright continues to represent peak Trump, up to and including the invention of his own system of mathematics. “The Trump Administration remains committed to reversing the misguided energy subtraction policies it inherited from past leaders,” Wright insisted in Friday afternoon’s order.

“Instead, we are advancing energy addition and expanding the American people’s access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity,” he emphasized.

Okay, sure. You do you, Chris. Good boy.

Meanwhile, just two days before Wright declared the latest “emergency,” the US Energy Information Energy announced that demand for coal in the power generation industry is subtracting, not adding.

Turns out, solar, wind, — especially solar — and energy storage are doing all the heavy lifting to keep the lights stay on. Who knew?

Photo: The J.H. Campbell coal power plant in Michigan will finally get taken off the life support, as a federal court rules that Energy Secretary Chris Wright overstepped his authority to keep the plant open past its scheduled retirement (cropped, courtesy of Consumers Energy).

text:
If the focus of Hyvolution Chile 2025 was laying the foundations for public policy, geopolitics, and attracting global investments, this year, the goal of Latin America's most important international green hydrogen and clean energy congress is moving to action, to project execution, financial viability, and the materialization of technologies on the ground.

Energy minister Ximena Rincón noted that while the country has unbeatable advantages for the sector, the challenge today is to turn tangible initiatives into reality with clear regulations, reasonable permit timelines, and a real impact on local employment and community wellbeing.

The minister detailed that the 2026-2030 Energy Roadmap translated this conviction into verifiable commitments. She highlighted the creation of an interministerial table for strategic energy investment to unblock timelines, the launch of a territorial logistics program for Magallanes, and the incorporation of the first hydrogen-powered bus assembled in Chile into the metropolitan transportation system by 2027.

"None of these announcements will produce a single metric ton of green hydrogen on its own, but together they determine whether that metric ton is produced here," she said.

“The most important aspect right now is that the factors hindering this industry's development have been evaluated extensively and consistently. The current stage involves resolving these barriers to advance execution more dynamically,” says Vivianne Blanlot, president of Hyvolution Chile 2026.

Meanwhile, Electricity and Fuels superintendent Marta Cabeza praised the role each actor is playing in the industry's takeoff. “Everyone involved, from civil society and the public sector to academia, contributes to developing this technology, which serves as a vital input for the country,” she said.

Matching supply with demand

In its fourth edition, Hyvolution Chile 2026 featured 15 main panels spread across the three days of the event, alongside keynotes, technical talks, sectoral agreement signings, and side events like the H2 Grand Prix, which involved students from technical and vocational institutions.

One of the standout panels was "R&D+i on H2 and derivatives: advances in Chile and the world," moderated by Rowena Moreno, a member of Corfo's Green Hydrogen Committee. Alongside experts and academic representatives, the panel included Leticia Frata, Sales Manager for Power Consulting at Hitachi Energy Brazil, the company's consulting unit that conducts feasibility studies and advises sector stakeholders on the electrical connection of their green hydrogen plants.

“Each project has specific characteristics and must therefore be structured from the prefeasibility stage, considering proper equipment sizing and grid integration studies,” says Moreno.

“Initiatives are being pushed forward quickly due to high expectations, but we have focused on having the product without ensuring we have the necessary input,” says Javier Quispe, director of the Department of Chemical Engineering at the Universidad Católica del Norte in Antofagasta. “Several projects have been developed, such as the Antofagasta locomotive, which requires hydrogen compressed at 350 bar, or vehicles requiring 700 bar, while current standard plant production exists at 30 bar.”

Leticia Frata says anticipating challenges related to power stability and quality is essential for selecting the most appropriate solutions, reducing risks, and supporting decisions that balance reliability, CAPEX, opex, and commercial viability. “In Brazil today, we have a project evaluating the origin of CO2, its quality, quantity, cost, and distance; evaluating all of this early on is crucial to guide investment decisions,” adding that this working experience can and likely will be replicated in the Chilean market.

Frata's statements align with the industry's transformation. This development is reflected in the international congress itself, which, starting in 2027, will be named Energyvolution, broadening its technological umbrella into a platform that more widely includes electrification, storage, new fuels, and renewable energies; aligned with Hitachi Energy's solutions for the energy transition, the executive said.

text:
A federal appeals court has ruled that the United States Energy Department exceeded its authority when it ordered a coal-fired power plant in the US state of Michigan to remain open beyond its planned retirement, dealing a setback to the Trump administration’s effort to keep ageing coal facilities operating.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled unanimously on Friday that there was no emergency under federal law that justified keeping the 64-year-old JH Campbell Generating Plant online. Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked emergency powers last year, arguing that the plant was needed to maintain reliable electricity in the region.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Long before Trump: How US policy has harmed the environment for decades

list 2 of 3Trump admin’s cancellation of wind energy projects causes business turmoil

list 3 of 3Powerful El Nino to intensify heat on ‘a planet already on fire’: UN

end of list

President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergency in an executive order in January last year, citing demand increases from artificial intelligence and data centre growth.

Judge Cornelia Pillard, writing for the three-judge panel, said the emergency provision of the Federal Power Act was intended as a “narrow, last-resort backstop.” She said the authority could be used only when immediate action was required, and states or utilities could not address the problem themselves.

Pillard also described the reversal of the plant’s “long and carefully planned retirement” as “disruptive”.

The plant, operated by Consumers Energy, had been scheduled to close in May 2025, but the company has continued operations under energy department orders. That has cost about $259m, according to financial filings, with opponents warning that the expense could ultimately fall on families and businesses in midwestern US states.

The company told The Associated Press it was reviewing the court ruling.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, a Democrat, whose office joined counterparts in Illinois and Minnesota in challenging the orders, welcomed the ruling. She said the appeals court had “thrown out DOE’s order that had zero basis in reality”.

The Energy Department defended its use of emergency powers, saying the orders helped prevent blackouts and “likely saved hundreds of lives” during periods of peak demand, particularly during severe winter storms in late January and early February.

The department said that during the winter storm peak, coal generation in affected areas increased by 25 percent compared to the previous year.

The Michigan case is one of several legal disputes that have emerged across the country. Secretary Wright issued another emergency order, just hours after the ruling, to a coal plant in Centralia, Washington, to remain in operation. Similar orders have been issued for plants in Indiana, Colorado and Florida, as well as an oil and gas plant in Pennsylvania.

text:
The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency released on Thursday, Sept. 10, the Illinois Comprehensive Climate Action Plan.

The report builds on the state’s Priority Climate Action Plan, which the agency submitted to U.S. EPA in 2024 as part of the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program. The Illinois EPA won a $430 million grant under the CPRG program to implement programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Following broad public outreach, the CCAP provides an actionable roadmap to meet Illinois’ carbon reduction goals.

Analysis in the Plan found that Illinois has reduced planet-warming greenhouse gas pollution by 32% since 2005, but more action will be needed to meet the state’s goal of net zero emissions by 2050. The plan models a set of policies that, if adopted by the General Assembly, would reduce emissions in the state by 72% from 2005 levels by 2050 and finds that implementing these policies would produce $21 billion per year in net benefits by 2050.

“Since the adoption of the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, Illinois has been a national leader in addressing carbon emissions, particularly from the energy and transportation sectors,” said Illinois EPA Director James Jennings. “The CCAP builds on these past successes by identifying a path for Illinois to achieve significant reductions in climate change-causing greenhouse gases and meet the state’s long term climate goals.”

“Illinoisans are seeing the extreme heat and storms climate change has brought to our doorstep this summer. We are feeling the high, unpredictable costs of fossil fuel every time we reach for our wallets,” said Illinois Climate Advisor JC Kibbey. “This plan shows the great progress we’ve made on climate and clean energy – and how much more we have left to do. We have the tools to achieve our state’s goal of a healthier, cleaner, safer, more affordable future – we only need to use them. The time to start is now.”

Illinois has made the most progress reducing emissions in the power sector, with a 60% reduction since 2005, mostly from transitioning away from coal and using lower-polluting sources of power generation. Illinois also cut transportation emissions by 24%, mostly from enhanced fuel efficiency standards and a growing number of electric vehicles on the road.

Illinois EPA developed the CCAP with extensive public input, including nine public listening sessions across the state, resulting in hundreds of survey responses and written comments from residents, organizations, and businesses.

The CCAP expands on greenhouse gas reduction measures included in Illinois’ CPRG proposal, including transportation, buildings, industry, and agriculture initiatives. CCAP strategies include:

Increasing incentives for electric vehicles to replace loss of federal incentives.

Reducing vehicle miles traveled by focusing new building construction in high density areas.

Reducing natural gas emissions from buildings through flexible standards.

Implementing all-electric new construction codes.

Expanding incentives for heat pumps and building envelope efficiency upgrades.

Electrifying lawn and landscape equipment.

Reducing GHG emissions from large manufacturing facilities through flexible standards.

Reducing emissions from cement production.

Replacing high global warming potential hydrofluorocarbons with less-warming alternatives.

Strengthening methane monitoring and emission reductions.

Expanding incentives for sustainable agriculture.

Reducing fugitive emissions from coal mining and the oil and gas industry.

The measures outlined within the CCAP set a clear path for Illinois. These actions, if adopted, will enable the state to meet our greenhouse reduction goals and provide benefits to residents through lower fuel costs and improved health benefits for generations to come.

title: NextEra Advances Duane Arnold Nuclear Restart With Federal Loan - MarketScale
description:
NextEra Energy is working to bring the Duane Arnold Energy Center near Cedar Rapids, Iowa, back online after the plant shut down in 2020 for economic reasons.
NextEra aims to begin producing electricity from the 615-megawatt plant by early 2029, Canary Media reported.

text:
NextEra Energy is working to bring the Duane Arnold Energy Center near Cedar Rapids, Iowa, back online after the plant shut down in 2020 for economic reasons. On September 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy said it closed a loan of up to $1.9 billion to NextEra to help finance the restart, according to Canary Media. The loan came through the department's Office of Energy Dominance Financing, the renamed Loan Programs Office.

A federal loan and a long-term buyer are both in place

Canary Media reported that NextEra signed a 25-year agreement last fall with Google to supply electricity from Duane Arnold, intended to support Google's cloud-computing and AI infrastructure in Iowa. NextEra aims to begin producing electricity from the 615-megawatt plant by early 2029, Canary Media reported.

Separately, CNBC reported that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approved a NextEra request allowing Duane Arnold to reconnect to the electric grid, and that NextEra's own filings to FERC put the earliest restart date at the fourth quarter of 2028. CNBC reported the plant would add more than 600 megawatts of capacity, an amount CNBC said could serve more than 400,000 homes; Canary Media separately described the project as supplying enough power for nearly 500,000 homes.

Part of a wider pattern of nuclear restarts

Duane Arnold is one of three shuttered U.S. nuclear plants that companies are working to restart with federal financing support, according to Canary Media. The Office of Energy Dominance Financing previously closed a $1 billion loan for Constellation Energy's Crane plant in Pennsylvania and a $1.52 billion loan for Holtec International's Palisades plant in Michigan, Canary Media reported. Holtec's Palisades project has faced delays and missed its original early-2026 target, but Canary Media reported the company began loading nuclear fuel into the reactor vessel last week.

CNBC reported that NextEra described the Duane Arnold restart as a capital-intensive process, with spending of as much as $100 million planned for 2025 alone. The company has placed orders for replacement transformers, which CNBC reported face supply constraints and could take about three years to deliver; the plant's cooling towers, administration building, and training center were also dismantled after the 2020 shutdown and need to be rebuilt.

What buyers evaluating this project should track

Neither Canary Media nor CNBC reported the total cost of the Duane Arnold restart, so it is not clear from their reporting what share of the project the federal loan covers versus what is supported by the Google agreement or other financing. Companies weighing large power commitments tied to nuclear restarts may want to track remaining regulatory approvals from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the pace of equipment delivery such as the replacement transformers, and whether the plant's targeted restart timeline of late 2028 to early 2029 holds, given the delays already seen at comparable projects like Palisades.

title: Can India Build a Resilient EV Supply Chain Without Closing the Materials Loop?
description:
