text:
Between a growing economy and a changing climate, our state is facing a growing list of electricity needs. To meet these challenges and the policies we have committed to, we must find ways to improve the resiliency of our electrical grid. Among potential solutions to these needs are battery energy storage systems, also known as ‘BESS’. These use large, rechargeable batteries to store excess energy for later use. They can then supply power when other energy sources are limited or may be unavailable. Batteries can also provide electricity during emergencies, especially in remote areas that do not have strong connections to the electrical grid. Access to batteries gives utilities flexibility in how they can respond to these high demand events and can reduce disruptions like power outages.

While BESS can be a viable solution to some of our energy problems, we recognize that people have concerns about safety and impacts. That’s why we’re studying the potential impacts of large-scale, standalone battery energy storage systems in a new programmatic environmental impact statement. It will also include potential approaches to mitigating impacts.

How will we study battery energy storage systems?

The process starts with scoping, which is when we determine what to study.

On Sept. 1, 2026, we began an extended 30-day scoping period. We released a document describing our planned approach to evaluating large-scale, standalone battery energy storage systems in Washington. Our goal is to produce a document that considers the best available science to assess impacts, reduce risk, and help guide future project siting and design. We would like to hear from you about what you think we should study.

Washington Puts Real Dollars Behind Space-Based Solar Power

This week, Helio highlighted new federal commitment to the SBSP sector that it believes validates the long-term thesis behind its orbital energy strategy. On August 31, 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy announced a new grant program funding space photovoltaics research and development. Helio intends to submit an application for the program as it works to advance its own SBSP technology.

Helio enters this moment with flight-proven credibility already in hand: since its founding in 2018, the Company has delivered hardware across four lunar missions and developed deployable mechanisms, antenna systems, and other space-qualified technologies for NASA and commercial space programs. It has also secured commercial contracts with two customers - Elysium, a cognitive microcity in Florida, and Poderosa S.A., one of the largest gold producers in Latin America - underscoring early commercial traction for its energy technology.

Fourth Patent Filing Strengthens Helio's Lunar IP Moat

Helio also announced its fourth patent filing, a U.S. provisional patent application filed with the United States Patent and Trademark Office on September 9, 2026. Developed by the Company's Heliospace subsidiary, the filing covers launcher technology designed to deploy scientific instruments from a lunar lander to multiple points across the surrounding surface in a single mission without repositioning the lander or relying on a separate rover. The underlying design already carries mission heritage, having been used in prior space missions, and the filing's scope extends beyond the Moon to cover instrument deployment from spacecraft, rovers, and other planetary platforms.

The filing is the latest output of Helio's IP program, led by Vikas Parti, Board Director and Head of Intellectual Property. The milestone carries added weight given that lunar hardware currently represents approximately 60% of Helio's overall business, reinforcing what management describes as a self-sustaining cycle where R&D fuels new hardware, hardware fuels new IP, and IP compounds long-term commercial value.

Southwest Investor Roadshow Set for September 15-17

Rounding out the week, Helio announced a four-city Southwest investor roadshow spanning Austin, Houston, Phoenix, and Scottsdale giving investors across the region direct, in-person access to management. The tour opens in Austin, one of the nation's fastest-growing hubs for technology and venture capital, before moving to Houston, where deep aerospace and energy expertise aligns closely with Helio's infrastructure mission, and concludes in the Phoenix-Scottsdale metro area, a region with a rapidly expanding aerospace and defense manufacturing base.

Members of Helio's executive and technical leadership team will be in attendance, including Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ed Cabrera, who brings more than 40 years of Wall Street experience, and Chief Technology Officer and Founder Greg Delory, whose background includes leadership roles at the NASA Lunar Science Institute and NASA's LADEE lunar mission at the NASA Ames Research Center. Throughout the roadshow, management intends to update investors on Helio's expansion to participation in five lunar missions, progress on residential and industrial demonstrations of its SBSP technology, and an estimated $12 million contract pipeline alongside recent capital markets initiatives, shareholder growth, and the Company's broader strategy to develop space-based power systems and advanced space mechanisms.

Momentum Across the Board

Taken together, this week's developments illustrate a Company executing on multiple fronts simultaneously: a rapidly strengthening federal tailwind for the SBSP industry, a growing and increasingly strategic intellectual property portfolio protecting its core lunar business, and an expanding, direct line to the investor community through its national roadshow strategy. Helio believes its combination of flight heritage, engineering depth, and disciplined capital markets execution positions the Company to compete for government-funded programs and help build the infrastructure that could power the next era of American energy while continuing to grow shareholder value.

The project, led by Coreshell Technologies, will build about 2 gigawatt‑hours of electrode manufacturing capacity and 1.5 gigawatt‑hours of cell assembly capacity in the United States. The initiative is expected to create more than 100 jobs across production, technical and administrative roles.

AM Batteries is contributing its dry‑coating process for cathode manufacturing, which eliminates solvent‑based wet coating and solvent‑recovery systems. The company says combining its Powder to Electrode platform with advanced material integration reduces capital and operating costs while enabling higher‑performance, lower‑cost cells for electric vehicle and defense applications.

“This project is about proving that a 100% domestically produced high‑performance battery cell can be cost‑competitive with mass‑market cells from Asia,” said Hieu Duong, CTO of AM Batteries. “By combining AMB’s platform with Coreshell’s MGS anode technology, we can lower cost, improve performance, and help build a globally competitive battery industry in the West.”

AM Batteries says its dry‑electrode process removes wet‑slurry casting, large drying ovens and toxic solvents, reducing electrode manufacturing capital costs by up to 40 per cent and operating costs by more than 50 per cent while lowering the carbon footprint of battery plants.

text:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.

ODESSA — The Public Utility Commission of Texas will consider approving the buildout of three 765-kilovolt transmission lines spanning nearly 800 miles — roughly the size of Texas’ largest congressional district — to deliver electricity to the oil and gas industry and support the state’s booming industrial sector.

The hearing will take place Friday at 9:30 a.m. and can be watched online.

The Certificates of Convenience and Necessity, filed by Oncor, AEP Texas and CPS Energy, propose a massive construction endeavor in Central and South Texas, stretching west through at least 40 counties.

Just last week, the five commissioners presiding over the Utility Commission approved two first-of-their-kind transmission lines in North Texas after hours of impassioned testimony from landowners and the oil and gas industry.

Altogether, the five transmission line proposals, designed by power grid managers at the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, are the state’s largest and most ambitious electricity infrastructure project.

The hearing comes as Public Utility Commission Chairman Thomas Gleeson on Wednesday recommended sending two of the proposals back to the agency’s administrative courts.

“At this time, I believe it is premature to address whether the recommendations in the PFD should be acted on,” Gleeson wrote in a letter to the other four commissioners, adding that the State Office of Administrative Hearings, which recommends the proposals commissioners vote on, issued an incomplete proposal for a decision. Gleeson wrote the court did not explain whether the proposals met federal reliability standards.

“The lack of a recommendation on this issue is puzzling,” he wrote.

The administrative court’s ruling is also missing how much consumers would save, should the commission approve the transmission lines.

The proposals have put the industrial sector at odds with landowners over whether the lines are needed, catching the attention of lawmakers — many of whom voted for the bill that called for a plan to serve the state’s energy needs — and who now say they didn’t expect the transmission line proposals to be the outcome of that mandate.

“I understand the proceedings are not just about infrastructure to you,” Commissioner Courtney Hjaltman told landowners at last Friday’s hearing, following the approval. “They’re about your land. They’re about something deeply personal. They’re about your heart … and we understand that. We appreciate your participation in the process. We recognize the importance of the decision before us, and we don’t take it lightly. We have to constitutionally weigh certain factors in making our decisions, and that’s what we’re doing.”

The lines have alarmed swaths of landowners across Texas who worry the construction could cause irreparable damage to their land. Hundreds have filed letters and challenges to the applications, hoping the Utility Commission will reject them.

Some said they did not get legally required advance notice of the proposals, an argument the transmission companies disputed. Landowners have also said the Utility Commission’s 180-day timeframe to process the applications is too short. Ultimately, commissioners sided with the transmission companies, saying the applicants followed the Utility Commission’s rules.

“I don’t feel the landowners have had the adequate time or the proper procedure to be able to deal with something of this magnitude,” said Jada Jo, president of the Hill Country Preservation Coalition, a landowner group opposing the transmission lines.

Trade groups representing the industrial sector and oil and gas industry have insisted the lines are necessary to support the state’s breakneck growth and that electricity needs have lagged for at least a decade. They’ve argued that there isn’t enough transmission infrastructure to support oil and gas production or the industrial manufacturing sector. Power generators that convert natural gas into electricity, meanwhile, argue that the transmission lines will spur the energy market to build more power plants and support the state’s energy grid, which Texas has historically struggled to do.

The fierce debate drew scrutiny in Austin, where the Texas Legislature has launched hours-long hearings on the issue. Over the summer, legislative committees in the House and Senate heard from landowners, several industries and the transmission companies.

After a 15-hour July hearing in the Senate Business and Commerce Committee, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the committee’s chair, called on the Utility Commission to reject every proposal so the Legislature could reform the application process. On X, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick echoed the calls.

“Everyone agrees Texas needs the transmission to meet the growing needs of the state,” Patrick wrote. “However, support for ERCOT’s 765kV transmission plan should not come at the expense of private property rights.”

State Rep. Ken King, R-Canadian, also asked the Utility Commission to reject the plan after presiding over an eight-hour hearing in the House State Affairs Committee.

text:
Abuja, Nigeria, 2 September 2026 – More than 160 stakeholders from Nigeria's mining, climate, energy and industrial sectors convened in Abuja to identify practical measures for leveraging critical minerals to advance green industrialisation, economic diversification and sustainable development, while supporting Nigeria's net-zero emissions objective by 2060.

The High-Level Stakeholder Convening on Advancing Nigeria's Green Industrialisation Through Critical Minerals was organised by the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) in collaboration with APRI - Africa Policy Research Institute, with support from the Ford Foundation. It brought together policymakers, industry leaders, investors, development partners, civil society organisations, researchers and other stakeholders to examine how Nigeria can translate its mineral endowment into industrial capability, investment, jobs and broader economic value.

Representing the Honourable Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Hon. Dr. Oladele Henry Alake, Engr. Faruk Yusuf Yabo, FNSE, Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development, highlighted the importance of defining critical minerals according to Nigeria's own development priorities. He noted that the Ministry, in partnership with the World Bank, has developed a critical minerals development roadmap for Nigeria.

"The strategic blueprint will define Nigeria's own priority critical minerals, since the concept of ‘critical mineral’ is relative to each nation's own priorities, and will map out how development, financing, compliance and enforcement will work."

He added that the roadmap, once launched, is expected to provide a strategic framework for critical minerals development in Nigeria and could offer lessons for the wider continent.

Representing the Honourable Minister of Environment, Malam Balarabe Abbas Lawal, Dr. Iniobong Abiola-Awe, Director, Department of Climate Change, Federal Ministry of Environment, emphasised that Nigeria's industrial ambitions must advance alongside strong environmental safeguards.

"Economic development and environmental protection are not competing objectives; both must advance together, and environmental protection cannot be negotiated away in pursuit of investment."

She stressed that Nigeria must build a critical minerals economy that is environmentally responsible, economically transformative, socially inclusive and nationally beneficial, while ensuring that investment aligns with the country's development and environmental objectives.

Delivering the keynote address, Dr. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), underscored the need to connect climate policy with Nigeria's wider economic and industrial ambitions.

"Our role is to ensure that Nigeria's climate policy supports, rather than sits separately from, the country's wider economic and industrial ambitions."

She noted that Nigeria's Nationally Determined Contributions, Energy Transition Plan, emerging carbon-market architecture and climate-finance ecosystem should ultimately help attract investment, create competitive industries and improve livelihoods.

Speaking on the role of development finance in the sector, Mr Abdulmajeed Musa, Technical Adviser, representing Hajia Fatima Umaru Shinkafi, Executive Secretary & CEO of the Solid Minerals Development Fund (SMDF), reaffirmed the Fund's commitment to strengthening Nigeria's mining ecosystem.

"The Solid Minerals Development Fund remains committed to supporting initiatives that strengthen Nigeria's mining ecosystem, mobilise responsible investment and translate our mineral resources into greater economic value creation."

He highlighted the need to move beyond conversations about mineral potential towards implementation, investment readiness and building industries around Nigeria's mineral resources.

Dr. Chichi Aniagolu, Regional Director, Ford Foundation, West Africa, emphasised the importance of cross-sector collaboration in shaping Nigeria's green industrialisation agenda.

"To build a blueprint for Nigeria's green energy revolution, we must enhance and strengthen collaboration across traditional silos and facilitate a rich exchange of knowledge, learning deeply from both international successes and our own domestic experiences. No single entity can achieve this alone. That is why this forum is intentionally designed to promote a fierce, transparent dialogue on governance, strategic investment, beneficiation, local value addition, and, crucially, long-term environmental sustainability and positive community outcomes."

Also speaking at the convening, Engr. Jaafar Dikko, Senior Adviser, Rural Electrification Agency (REA), representing Dr. Abba Abubakar Aliyu, MD/CEO of the REA, highlighted the role of Nigeria's growing energy market in supporting domestic industrialisation.

"Nigeria's mineral endowment is one half of the equation. The REA and other energy-service providers bring the other half, a guaranteed and scalable domestic market."

He noted that growing demand for solar panels, batteries, inverters, meters and other clean-energy technologies could provide an anchor for local manufacturing, technology transfer, skilled jobs and stronger domestic supply chains.

Dr. Olumide Abimbola, Executive Director of APRI - Africa Policy Research Institute, situated the discussion within the wider geopolitical competition for critical minerals and global supply chains.

"Global competition for critical minerals is intensifying. Nigeria needs to understand where its leverage lies, how it engages international partners, and what it should be negotiating for beyond extraction."

He emphasised that critical minerals sit at the intersection of climate, energy, industrial policy, trade, finance, geopolitics, community development and environmental protection, and present an opportunity for Nigeria to connect its climate ambitions with its wider development objectives.

The convening featured three thematic panel sessions examining Nigeria's Minerals in a Shifting Global Order; Building Nigeria's Critical Minerals Ecosystem for Green Industrialisation; and Protecting Community and Environmental Rights in Mining Communities in Nigeria.

Across the discussions, participants highlighted the need to strengthen Nigeria's negotiating position, improve geological information and investment readiness, expand domestic processing and manufacturing, mobilise appropriate finance, support the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining, and embed community and environmental safeguards from the outset.

The convening reinforced a central message: Nigeria's critical minerals opportunity extends beyond what is extracted from the ground. Its long-term value will depend on how effectively the country converts its mineral resources into competitive industries, investment, technology, skilled jobs, stronger Nigerian businesses and lasting benefits for communities.

title: Texas has lessons for powering Europe - POLITICO
description:
Surge Preview Texas knows how to handle skyrocketing power demand.
Second, Texas prices its power differently.
“China remains the dominant driver of global coal demand — and this is unlikely to change for some time.
Coal demand is expected to fall in Europe and the U.S. “In the European Union, coal demand is set to continue its structural decline, although the fall is now expected to be less pronounced than previously anticipated,” the IEA said.
DEADLINE SLIP: Trump said Wednesday that the Iran war will end and gas prices will plummet “immediately after” November’s midterm elections, writes Scott Waldman.
text:
With help from Brian Dabbs in Singapore, Charlie Cooper in the United Kingdom, Corbin Hiar, Sara Schonhardt and Zack Colman in the U.S., Zia Weise in Belgium, Mike Blanchfield in Canada, and Nicolas Camut in France.

Surge Preview

Texas knows how to handle skyrocketing power demand. Europe should listen.

Virginia’s lieutenant governor talks with Surge about voters’ queasiness with data centers.

Coal is on the rise, and clean energy investment is not.

FASTEST POWER IN THE WEST: Soaring electricity demand is a new phenomenon on both sides of the Atlantic. But it’s an old story in Texas.

That makes the Lone Star State a case study for how the world can meet rising power demand without breaking the bank, especially at a time when political leaders are scrambling to stave off rate hikes. And, in a twist, America’s oil and gas capital has done it by becoming a global leader in solar and batteries.

Demand growth in the Lone Star State has grown four times faster than the U.S. average over the last decade. Yet most Texans still pay less for their electricity than other Americans.

Many grids in North America and Europe face a new challenge stemming from the explosion of data centers and electric vehicles: Power demand is growing faster than supply. That’s pushing up prices.

Texas is different, because it builds power plants fast.

“If you just let people build stuff, generally speaking, they’ll build the right stuff,” said Michael Webber, a professor at the University of Texas-Austin who studies electricity markets. “And by the right stuff, I mean things that are economic, things that are clean, things that are available when you need them. That’s the fundamental feature of Texas.”

Call it the Texas two-step.

First, the state makes it easy to plug into the grid. Most grid operators require new power plants to undergo intensive periods of study to see if transmission upgrades are needed to accommodate the new electricity output.

Not in Texas. Instead, its grid operator tells developers that their planned plants might be asked to ramp down generation if existing power lines are maxed out during certain periods of the day. That leads to plants being built faster.

Second, Texas prices its power differently. It uses a nodal system, with every substation across the grid having its own wholesale price. High prices signal congestion or high demand, while low prices signal ample supply.

That’s in stark contrast to countries like Germany and the U.K., which use one national wholesale price for power. Advocates say Texas’ approach aids grid expansion by sending developers a powerful economic signal.

“You know what the prices will be where and when, and that’s really useful because then you can get a sense of what to build, where to build it,” said Webber, who formerly worked at the French utility Engie.

Some of Texas’ policy moves are being used in other markets. The United Kingdom and, more recently, the European Union have adopted similar flexible interconnection approaches when plugging in new power plants.

But the practice has become controversial in the U.K., where the slow pace of transmission upgrades has resulted in billions of pounds being spent each year to compensate wind farms in Scotland for powering down while gas plants in England are paid to ramp up.

That points to the limits of the Texas analogy.

Few regions can emulate its abundance of wind, solar and natural gas. And market structures alone are not enough to meet demand growth. Interconnection processes need to be harmonized with permitting to move major projects forward.

That’s easier in places like Texas, where the grid sits entirely within the state, said Michael Caravaggio, vice president of fleet reliability and environment at the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit.

Even then it can be difficult. Texas utility regulators recently approved two new transmission lines despite widespread protests from rural residents and some state lawmakers.

It’s even harder on grids that cross state and country lines (like the PJM Interconnection in the mid-Atlantic U.S. and the European Union). In the EU, member countries and lawmakers have been arguing for nearly a year over how to plan a pan-European grid that’s fit for the EU’s ambitious electrification goals, with no agreement yet in sight.

The world still has a lot to learn from Texas, said Georg Rute, an Estonian who worked for his country’s grid operator before moving to Austin, Texas, to run the power services firm Gridraven.

By making it easier to build new infrastructure, the state has provided a template for how to meet rising electricity demand at a time when some analysts are predicting Texas could overtake Virginia as the data center capital of the world. And it’s being done in a way that might make European leaders green with envy.

No state in the U.S. boasts a larger renewable fleet. Wind and solar are the second- and third-largest electricity generators on the Texas grid, trailing only natural gas.

Texas shows that “the cheapest way to power and meet load growth is to build solar and wind as much as you can and to have gas backup,” Rute said.

WELCOME TO SURGE: I’m Benjamin Storrow, your lead author and trend-tracking journalist. Send tips, ideas and international energy intel to bstorrow@politico.com.

Power Players

VIBE CHECK: Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi has been packing rooms across the Old Dominion this summer, as part of an energy listening tour aimed at getting voters’ feedback on NextEra Energy’s proposed $67 billion takeover of Dominion Energy, the state’s largest utility.

Surge asked Hashmi, a Democrat elected last year, what she’s hearing about electricity prices and the explosion of data centers. The conversation has been edited for brevity.

What are voters saying?

It is different than on the campaign trail last summer. This summer, I feel like there’s just a lot of anxiety. People want to come to these town halls. They are sharing frustrations. They’re sharing how anxious they are, especially our seniors on fixed income, and how challenging it is right now to face all of the financial burdens. And so, I think this level of anxiety is very different this year compared to what I had seen on the campaign trail just a year ago.

Last week we saw Microsoft challenge a new Virginia rule requiring data centers to pay for the costs of transmission upgrades. That seems in contrast to tech companies’ pledges to pay for the cost of their infrastructure. Does Virginia need to do more to protect ratepayers?

Well, I think we need to revisit our standards of approval with the SCC [the state utility regulator]. Some of them are almost 100 years old at this point, and certainly the dramatic changes that we’ve seen in technology, in the energy sector, are making many of the demands even more complex. And so, I think we need to revisit all of our regulatory standards in that regard.

At the federal level, the midterm election season is kicking into high gear. Democrats have been pounding this message about being opposed to data centers. Virginia is home to the largest collection of data centers in the world. Is it closed for business or is there still room for building more?

Yeah, I think it’s much more nuanced here in Virginia. As you said, we are the data center capital of the world, and there is a reason for that. You know, our close proximity to critical national security facilities and interests is a logical reason for Virginia to be playing such a strong role. The data center industry has brought a lot of jobs and great economic development for many of our localities.

I think what Virginia is going to be focused on, and again, I’m hearing this from our legislative community, is that we need to have a greater statewide perspective on the siting, the permitting. We need to have full data on the environmental impacts, the impacts on our electric system.

So I would personally like to see a strong balance where we have greater statewide perspective on all of the necessary impacts that we are seeing, that we are integrating the opportunities for communities and residents to have a strong voice in the process of permitting, and make sure that the decision is balancing between effective economic development, job creation and ensuring that we aren’t putting these complexes in the backyards — literally the backyards of many residences. — Benjamin Storrow

Driving the (global!) day

HELLO AGAIN, COAL: Global coal demand is set to rise 1.2% this year as Asia grapples with high gas prices, the International Energy Agency said Thursday.

“Higher natural gas prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East, made coal more cost-competitive for power generation, supporting coal demand,” the IEA outlined in a new report.

Coal demand is forecast to rise this year in India, South Korea, China, Southeast Asia and elsewhere, the IEA said, even as global coal production is expected to decline. Spot liquefied natural gas prices in Asia hit a four-year high last week, according to Bloomberg.

“China remains the dominant driver of global coal demand — and this is unlikely to change for some time. The country’s power sector will continue to determine the trajectory of coal demand,” the report said.

Coal demand is expected to fall in Europe and the U.S.

“In the European Union, coal demand is set to continue its structural decline, although the fall is now expected to be less pronounced than previously anticipated,” the IEA said.

On Wednesday, the European TTF benchmark price briefly rose above the €80 per megawatt-hour mark, a threshold not crossed since the winter of 2023.

“As with demand, the outlook for coal production in 2027 will depend on the evolution of the conflict in the Middle East,” the report said. “If LNG flows through the Strait recover, global coal production is expected to increase by around 0.3%, reflecting a rebound in production in China after this year’s decline.” — Brian Dabbs

IT’S NOT EASY BEING GREEN: Global clean energy investment is down 17 percent during the first half of the year, according to a report released Thursday by the Rhodium Group and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Electric power and transportation, the two largest segments of global clean energy spending, were both down. Investment in clean power fell 31% in the first quarter before rebounding 6% in the second quarter, compared to the same time last year. Spending on EVs was down 29% in the first quarter, but rose 8% in the second quarter.

China drove the decline in both categories, the report said. Beijing ended tax exemptions on EV purchases and overhauled its power market in January. That means wind and solar projects will now have to sell their electricity on the wholesale market like other forms of generation. The price had been previously set by the state.

The switch led to a crush of clean energy projects in 2025, as developers rushed to finish new facilities before the change — Benjamin Storrow

U.N. BACKS CARBON REMOVAL: The United Nations says it’s time for governments to embrace high-tech efforts to remove heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

The timing: It comes as rising energy demand from artificial intelligence and other technological advances threatens to push the planet past a warming limit set by the Paris Agreement.

The appeal: “Keeping 1.5ºC within reach requires climate policy to evolve to include the removal of already emitted” climate pollution, the U.N. Environment Programme said last week in a major climate report that suggested 1.8 degrees is a more realistic goal. It called for governments to establish “new policy frameworks and institutions to scale [carbon dioxide removal], manage long-term removal obligations and provide clear investment signals to the private sector.”

The response: UNEP’s new embrace of carbon removal is unlikely to move Washington, where President Donald Trump has dismissed climate change as a “hoax” and held up funding for direct air capture, a type of carbon removal. But it could provide new momentum in Brussels, Ottawa and other capitals.

“It opens up opportunities in California,” according to Will Kain, CEO of the Los Angeles-based direct air capture startup Avnos. The report “provides further support for every other federal jurisdiction in the world that has been moving in the direction of more decarbonization.”

Existing efforts: Even before the report’s release, some governments had already begun to support the development of carbon removal.

The EU has a blocwide certification framework for carbon removal and in July proposed integrating certain types of removal credits into its emissions trading system. Canada offers generous subsidies for direct air capture and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney is moving to procure carbon removals and establish national removal goals. — Corbin Hiar

HOUTHIS, TRUMP AND OIL: Global oil prices are showing no signs of easing. Having cleared the $100 per barrel mark on Wednesday, Brent crude briefly rose above $105 on Thursday. An offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen, which has seen them seize the Red Sea port of Mocha and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, has sparked fears that Red Sea trade routes could be threatened, analysts said. Prices weren’t helped by Trump saying the Iran war will carry on past the U.S. midterm elections. — Charlie Cooper

Our open tabs

OFF COURSE: EU members have barely used a fifth of the €300 billion in emergency grants and loans made available by the European Commission to turbocharge renewable energy and diversify the continent’s energy supplies in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ben Munster reports.

I DRINK YOUR MILKSHAKE: The water wars are heating up in Texas. Historically, anyone in the Lone Star State with a private well could consume as much H2O as they wanted. The thing is: That same rule also applies to data centers — and that’s making some people mad. Data centers are squaring off with local conservation districts over water usage, which has state lawmakers pondering a change to Texas’ 120-year-old water laws, Shelby Webb reports today.

DEADLINE SLIP: Trump said Wednesday that the Iran war will end and gas prices will plummet “immediately after” November’s midterm elections, writes Scott Waldman. That prediction would ensure Republican candidates will continue to contend with the conflict’s impacts on the cost of living — a topic that is rattling attendees at this week’s GOP convention, as Meredith Lee Hill, Erin Doherty, Alec Hernandez and Andrew Howard report. The price of oil hit $100 per barrel earlier this week, following new military strikes against Iran.

That’s all for today! Thanks for reading!

text:
The Trump administration is poised to loosen environmental restrictions on oil and gas wells that produce very little energy but release vast amounts of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas.

The Environmental Protection Agency is proposing to drastically weaken requirements for leak inspections and equipment upgrades at more than 700,000 low-producing “stripper wells,” according to a draft rule being reviewed by the White House and seen by ProPublica. These wells — which tend to be old, poorly maintained and thus prone to leaking — produce just 6% of the country’s oil and natural gas but are responsible for roughly half the sector’s methane pollution, studies show.

The EPA acknowledged similar figures in the draft. But it said that the cost of complying with existing regulations would force the lowest-producing wells to shut down and that this was “unreasonable” — even though it would eliminate just 0.4% of U.S. oil and gas production, according to an industry estimate cited in the proposed rule.

The proposal, which would also weaken methane controls in the wider oil industry, is expected to save companies $42 billion through 2050. An attached memo says the rollback will help to “unleash” American energy, one of President Donald Trump’s favorite slogans.

Environmental advocates said deregulating stripper wells will do little to boost energy output while significantly increasing climate pollution.

“This is not about energy dominance,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group. “It’s about padding the pockets of oil and gas operators and saddling society with the costs.”

The proposed changes are the culmination of a campaign by a previously low-profile faction of the oil industry that has gained unprecedented influence during the second Trump administration. In the draft, the EPA said it is deregulating stripper wells — defined as those that produce up to 15 barrels a day — in response to petitions from the Independent Petroleum Association of America and the National Stripper Well Association, among other groups.

As ProPublica reported in June, the IPAA has long enjoyed the support of a little-known oil billionaire named Jeffery Hildebrand. He is the founder and owner of Hilcorp, a privately held company known for buying up old, poorly maintained stripper wells — a business that was threatened when the Biden administration imposed aggressive restrictions on methane pollution in 2024.

In response, Hildebrand became one of the oil industry’s biggest Trump donors. Trump, back in office, promptly appointed a former Hilcorp lobbyist named Aaron Szabo to a top post at the EPA, putting him in charge of the effort to unravel the new methane rules.

Szabo had previously helped to draft a letter on behalf of the American Exploration and Production Council — which has Hilcorp’s CEO on its board — opposing those rules. He also gave advice on climate regulations for Project 2025, the deregulatory roadmap for the current administration.

Among Project 2025’s recommendations: eliminate an EPA program that would track “super-emitter” events — enormous methane releases that have long plagued the oil industry — and would oblige companies to respond to them. The AXPC and the IPAA have also called for an end to the program.

And the current proposal from Trump’s EPA aims to do just that.

An IPAA spokesperson declined to comment on the group’s influence in the Trump administration but said in an emailed statement that its lobbying “has focused on ensuring regulations are workable for low-production and marginal wells.”

The NSWA and AXPC didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment. NSWA representatives previously told ProPublica that they had asked the EPA to soften restrictions on stripper wells because many of their members couldn’t afford the compliance costs. AXPC CEO Anne Bradbury previously told ProPublica that the group’s members were “committed to building on a legacy of world-leading methane emission reductions.”

Hilcorp spokesperson Nick Piatek didn’t provide a comment either but previously told ProPublica that the company was “proud” of recent efforts to reduce its emissions.

While Szabo didn’t respond to emails from ProPublica, the EPA’s press office said in a statement that he “had not done any work for AXPC for well over a year before he started working for the federal government” and that he had reviewed federal ethics rules with the agency’s ethics staff upon joining. The agency declined to comment on the substance of the methane rule revisions except to confirm that they were being reviewed by the White House Office of Management and Budget. The OMB’s press office didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment.

The rules now being rolled back were a key component of former President Joe Biden’s ambitious climate agenda. They would have cut methane pollution from the oil industry by 80%, the EPA said at the time. Because methane breaks down relatively quickly — in about a dozen years — cutting these emissions is one of the few known ways to reduce global warming in our lifetimes. Methane accounts for one-third of the rise in temperatures since the Industrial Revolution, according to the United Nations Environment Programme.

Since methane is the main component of natural gas, the rules would also have prevented useful energy from being lost to the atmosphere in the form of leaks and other releases. All told, Biden’s EPA had valued the rules’ climate, health and energy benefits at more than $7 billion a year, even after accounting for increased compliance costs.

Breaking with precedent, Trump’s EPA didn’t include calculations of the environmental and health impacts of the new proposal. But if it goes into effect, much of the public benefit will evaporate while oil and gas producers see increased profits.

title: Trump pulled the plug on EVs. Georgia EV makers are adapting and forging ahead
authors: Emily Jones, WABE/Grist, Emily Jones, Alander Rocha
description:
Georgia went all out with tax breaks and a worker training program to attract EV and battery makers — and it’s worked.
And in 2025, Rivian broke ground on its manufacturing plant near Atlanta.
Georgia leads the region in EV and battery manufacturing, but the growth has stumbled, with layoffs at SK Battery earlier this year.
Despite actively pursuing EV manufacturing, Georgia doesn’t have incentives to encourage EV adoption like some other states.
Valdez-Streaty believes that, over time, making EVs in Georgia will likely lead to more people in Georgia buying them.
text:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.

A year ago this month, federal immigration agents raided an electric vehicle battery plant in coastal Georgia and arrested more than 400 people, most of them South Korean workers there to help get the new factory off the ground.

It was a grim moment in what has been a challenging year-and-a-half for the industry in Georgia. But the EV makers are still forging ahead, even if that means making some adjustments.

For years, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp has been working to make the state a welcoming home for clean-energy manufacturing, including EVs, solar panels and batteries. Georgia went all out with tax breaks and a worker training program to attract EV and battery makers — and it’s worked.

Georgia-based bus manufacturer Blue Bird started selling electric buses commercially in 2018 and built an expanded factory for electric buses in 2023. In 2022, Hyundai built a plant near Savannah that it said would be dedicated to making EVs. In 2024, Kia started making EVs at its West Point plant. And in 2025, Rivian broke ground on its manufacturing plant near Atlanta. The Hyundai and Rivian operations are two of the biggest economic development projects in Georgia history. The state has also worked to attract other parts of the EV and clean energy manufacturing sector, including battery makers and recyclers and solar panel companies.

Under the second Trump administration, the economic outlook for these companies has been destabilized. In addition to ending federal EV tax credits for car buyers, the Trump administration has imposed tariffs on battery packs, charger hardware and other components; loosened rules around emissions from gas-powered cars; and ended the Biden administration’s push to make government vehicle fleets electric.

Factories adjust

At Kia’s plant in West Point, a long and constantly varied line of vehicles moves steadily forward on the assembly line, step by step gaining all the trimmings that turn metal shells into driveable cars.

This plant functions more like a short-order cook than a traditional assembly line. Instead of producing big, uniform batches, Kia has designed the plant to manufacture cars according to unique specifications — each one a different model, color or trim. There are gas-powered, hybrid and electric cars rolling off the line here. Kia says it has done this to make more of the cars people most want to buy at any given moment.

Right now, that means hybrids.

“What we’ve seen is a transition back away from maybe full EV vehicle building to this kind of a middle-of-the-road opportunity,” said factory CEO Stuart Countess.

Electric cars are still the future, he said. But for several reasons, including price and charging access, consumers just aren’t there yet. Changes to federal policy are a major factor, too.

“We had a tax incentive credit that did go away,” Countess said. “Sales were really moving in the right direction, but once it went away, it became a much different environment.”

Just as Kia has ramped up hybrid production, its sister company Hyundai has added hybrid production to the lineup produced at its massive plant near Savannah, which was originally built to make EVs.

“It’s kind of a messy period we’re in right now,” said Stephanie Valdez-Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive. “But I think the manufacturers are adjusting.”

At the same time, battery makers throughout the state have started shifting to producing storage batteries for electricity storage in addition to ones made to power vehicles.

“The state continues to have a lot riding on the success of both the electric vehicle but also the battery market,” said Stan Cross of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, or SACE.

Georgia leads the region in EV and battery manufacturing, but the growth has stumbled, with layoffs at SK Battery earlier this year. More than $4 billion in investment has been canceled or scaled back in the last year across the Southeast, according to SACE – though that’s dwarfed by the nearly $74 billion in manufacturing investment that’s moving ahead.

Making vs. buying EVs

One open question, Cross said, is whether Georgians will buy the hybrids and EVs being made in the state. Despite actively pursuing EV manufacturing, Georgia doesn’t have incentives to encourage EV adoption like some other states. In fact, there’s an extra registration fee designed to make up for lost gas taxes.

“When it comes to electric vehicles, Georgia politics remains utterly confused,” Cross said.

Private investment continues, though, including in charging infrastructure — a key missing piece for many car buyers considering going electric.

Kia and Hyundai are part of a charging consortium called IONNA that has installed several charging stations around the state, including one at the Kia factory site in West Point. Electric utilities are investing more in vehicle charging too. Across the region, EV-related investment by utilities increased by 14% this year, according to SACE.

“Though we’re not seeing a lot of activity on the legislative side, we do see potential on the regulatory side and really are encouraging Georgia Power to step up and help kind of fill the void that policymakers in the state are creating,” Cross said.

Valdez-Streaty believes that, over time, making EVs in Georgia will likely lead to more people in Georgia buying them.

“It’s like that familiarity, right?” she said. “People have jobs at those companies and familiarity with those products.”

Though shaky for the last 18 months or so, she said the EV market is starting to stabilize — and the auto industry is still going electric, it’s just taking a little longer.

title: New US plant makes lithium carbonate from 100% recycled batteries - Interesting Engineering
description:
R3 Lithium has started producing lithium carbonate from recycled battery materials at its facility in Covington, Georgia.
The company expects the Georgia facility to produce more than half of US lithium carbonate output in 2027.
R3 processes that material at the same site to recover lithium and produce lithium carbonate.
Scrap and spent batteries can enter the facility and emerge as refined lithium carbonate.
If its expansion targets hold, recycled batteries could become a larger source of domestically produced lithium carbonate in the US.
text:
R3 Lithium has started producing lithium carbonate from recycled battery materials at its facility in Covington, Georgia.

The 154,000-square-foot plant is designed to recover lithium at commercial scale. R3 also raised $15 million in Series A funding to upgrade the operation.

The company expects the Georgia facility to produce more than half of US lithium carbonate output in 2027. Its existing production line can make 2,500 metric tons of lithium carbonate annually.

Georgia plant targets scale

The facility can shred as much as 30,000 metric tons of battery material each year. That feedstock includes manufacturing scrap and batteries reaching the end of their useful lives.

Shredding produces black mass, which contains the valuable materials left inside lithium-ion batteries. R3 processes that material at the same site to recover lithium and produce lithium carbonate.

The process combines calciner-based crystallization with water-based precipitation. Keeping those steps together eliminates the need to ship lithium-bearing material elsewhere for refining.

The facility previously produced 99%-pure lithium carbonate using entirely recycled material. R3 acquired the site in July after its previous owner invested about $150 million into the operation.

A second 2,500-metric-ton production line could eventually double the site’s lithium carbonate capacity. R3 has also secured roughly $1 billion in offtake agreements with customers.

More from Energy

See All

Trafigura is among the buyers supporting those agreements. Tim Wood-Dow, a battery metals trader at Trafigura, said domestic lithium supplies remain limited.

Recycling cuts supply chain

The approach could give US battery manufacturers another source of domestically processed lithium. Much of the world’s battery production and processing capacity remains overseas.

Developing new lithium mines also takes considerable time. Projects can spend seven to 10 years navigating permitting before production begins.

Recycling existing batteries offers a different route to supply. R3 can source lithium from material already circulating through the battery economy.

Demand for lithium carbonate is also expanding as battery storage grows. Global battery storage installations surpassed 300 gigawatt-hours during 2025.

Data center construction has added another source of demand for large energy storage systems. Each gigawatt-hour of grid-scale storage requires about 880 tons of lithium carbonate.

R3 plans to build additional facilities across North America and Europe. Each site would use modular production units capable of processing 5,000 metric tons annually.

The company plans to secure customer offtake agreements before deploying those units. That strategy would let R3 expand capacity in stages as demand develops.

One site handles recovery

The Covington facility also recovers materials beyond lithium. Its process produces concentrated metal oxide containing nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite.

R3 can sell those materials separately after extracting the lithium. That creates additional value from the same recycled battery feedstock.

Keeping the process on one site also reduces the number of locations involved in moving battery materials through the recycling chain. Scrap and spent batteries can enter the facility and emerge as refined lithium carbonate.

R3 now wants to replicate that model across additional sites. If its expansion targets hold, recycled batteries could become a larger source of domestically produced lithium carbonate in the US.

The global Battery Recycling Equipment Market is estimated to be valued at USD 1.62 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 5.9 billion by 2036, expanding at a CAGR of 13.8% during the forecast period. The market was valued at USD 1.42 billion in 2025. The report provides a comprehensive evaluation of the rapidly evolving battery recycling equipment market by examining market trends, recycling technology developments, electric vehicle adoption, battery manufacturing expansion, critical-material recovery, regulatory initiatives, competitive activities, and future growth opportunities across the automotive, energy storage, electronics, battery materials, and recycling industries.

Battery recycling equipment has emerged as an important solution for collecting, discharging, dismantling, shredding, sorting, processing, and recovering valuable materials from spent batteries and battery manufacturing scrap. The market includes battery collection and handling systems, discharge equipment, automated dismantling and robotic disassembly systems, crushers and shredders, magnetic and eddy-current separators, sensor-based sorting equipment, black mass processing systems, hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processing equipment, direct recycling systems, material recovery and refining equipment, environmental and safety systems, and automation and process-control solutions. These systems recover critical materials such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, copper, aluminum, and graphite from lithium-ion, lead-acid, nickel-based, and emerging battery chemistries. The rapid growth in electric vehicle adoption, increasing volumes of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, expanding battery manufacturing scrap, construction of gigafactories, government-backed investments, and the increasing focus on closed-loop battery supply chains are driving market growth worldwide.

This report delivers an in-depth assessment of the market by analyzing equipment innovations, recycling process developments, battery chemistry and form-factor requirements, feedstock availability, recovered-material economics, environmental and safety standards, plant capacity, investment activities, and competitive strategies shaping industry growth. It evaluates how advances in sorting and separation, automated dismantling, battery crushing and shredding, black mass processing, hydrometallurgical recovery, pyrometallurgical processing, direct recycling, cathode regeneration, lithium recovery, and robotic process control are improving safety, throughput, recovery rates, material purity, energy efficiency, and recycling economics. The study also provides strategic market forecasts, segment-level insights, and regional analysis to support informed business, investment, equipment procurement, plant design, technology selection, and battery supply-chain decisions.

Market Dynamics

The rapid growth in electric vehicle adoption remains one of the primary drivers of the battery recycling equipment market. Increasing sales of electric cars, buses, commercial vehicles, two-wheelers, and other electrified transportation systems are expanding the installed base of lithium-ion batteries that will eventually require end-of-life processing. Electric vehicle production is also generating substantial demand for battery cells, modules, and packs, which creates an immediate stream of manufacturing scrap during factory commissioning, yield improvement, and production ramp-up. As battery volumes increase, recycling companies, automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, and material recovery organizations are investing in equipment for disassembly, shredding, separation, black mass processing, and critical-material recovery.

The growing volume of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries is further accelerating market adoption. Batteries from early electric vehicle deployments, consumer electronics, power tools, and energy storage systems are increasingly entering collection and recycling channels. These batteries contain valuable materials that can be recovered and reintroduced into battery production, while improper handling can create safety, environmental, and fire risks. The need to process diverse battery packs safely and economically is increasing demand for automated discharge, dismantling, robotic handling, crushing, shredding, sorting, and refining systems capable of managing different chemistries, formats, sizes, and states of charge.

Expanding battery manufacturing capacity and gigafactory construction are also supporting market growth. Battery manufacturing scrap can be substantial during production ramp-up because of yield losses, process qualification, equipment commissioning, and quality-control requirements. This manufacturing scrap provides a near-term feedstock stream for recycling equipment even before large volumes of end-of-life electric vehicle batteries reach the market. As battery manufacturers expand production of lithium-ion cells for electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and stationary energy storage, demand is increasing for co-located or integrated recycling systems capable of handling electrode scrap, defective cells, modules, and other production waste.

Government-backed investment and regulatory initiatives are reshaping the competitive landscape. Governments are introducing policies, funding programs, recycling targets, extended producer responsibility requirements, critical-material strategies, and local-content incentives to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing and recycling capacity. Public investment in battery recycling research and infrastructure is supporting the development of direct recycling, hydrometallurgical processing, automated disassembly, and material-refining technologies. Regulatory attention to lithium-ion battery transport, storage, fire safety, hazardous waste, material recovery, and carbon reduction is further encouraging battery manufacturers and recyclers to adopt specialized equipment and compliant processing infrastructure.

The growing focus on critical-material security and closed-loop supply chains is increasing demand for advanced recovery equipment. Lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, copper, aluminum, and graphite are essential inputs for battery production, and their supply can be affected by mining constraints, geographic concentration, price volatility, geopolitical risks, and environmental concerns. Recycling equipment enables battery manufacturers and automotive OEMs to recover materials from manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries and use them in new battery production. Closed-loop models can reduce dependence on primary raw materials, shorten supply chains, improve material traceability, and support sustainability goals.

Continuous technological innovation is reshaping the market. Equipment manufacturers and recycling companies are developing automated robotic disassembly, machine-vision sorting, AI-enabled process monitoring, high-throughput shredders, advanced black mass processing, chemistry-specific separation systems, direct cathode regeneration, relithiation, hydrometallurgical extraction, pyrometallurgical recovery, and integrated environmental and safety solutions. Improvements in automation, sensor technology, process control, battery identification, material purity, energy efficiency, and fire prevention are helping recyclers address higher throughput and more diverse feedstock streams. Furthermore, direct recycling technologies that preserve cathode structures rather than breaking materials down into base elements are expected to create new growth opportunities.

Despite favorable market conditions, several challenges continue to influence industry adoption. High capital costs, complex battery chemistries, diverse cell and pack form factors, hazardous-material handling requirements, fire and thermal-runaway risks, uncertain feedstock availability, and fluctuating recovered-material prices remain important considerations affecting market expansion. Recycling equipment must be designed to safely process NMC, NCA, LFP, LCO, LMO, lead-acid, nickel-based, and emerging battery chemistries, as well as cylindrical, prismatic, pouch, module, and pack formats. Mixed feedstock streams can increase equipment complexity and reduce process optimization, while the need for chemistry-specific systems may raise capital requirements and operating costs for recyclers.

The market nevertheless presents substantial long-term opportunities. Expansion of closed-loop battery recycling, increasing adoption of direct recycling, growth of automated and robotic disassembly, rising investments in lithium and critical-material recovery, increasing use of battery recycling systems at gigafactory sites, and the development of dedicated equipment for emerging chemistries are expected to create favorable conditions for future market growth. The transition toward large-scale electric vehicle and energy storage deployment is expected to provide a substantial long-term feedstock base, while government support for domestic battery materials processing is encouraging regional recycling infrastructure. As battery manufacturers, automotive OEMs, and recyclers continue to emphasize resource security, safety, sustainability, cost reduction, and circularity, demand for advanced battery recycling equipment is expected to increase significantly across developed and emerging markets.

Segment Analysis

The report provides detailed market analysis across equipment type, recycling process, battery type, battery form factor, feedstock, recovered material, capacity, end user, and geography, enabling stakeholders to identify high-growth business opportunities and evolving battery circularity and materials recovery trends.

Based on equipment type, the market is segmented into battery collection, handling and discharge equipment, battery dismantling equipment, battery crushing and shredding equipment, sorting and separation equipment, black mass processing equipment, hydrometallurgical processing equipment, pyrometallurgical processing equipment, direct recycling equipment, material recovery and refining equipment, environmental and safety equipment, and automation, robotics and process-control equipment. Sorting and separation equipment currently accounts for the largest share of market revenue owing to its critical role in isolating recoverable materials and battery chemistries across mixed feedstock streams through magnetic, eddy-current, density, optical, and sensor-based technologies. Direct recycling equipment is expected to register the fastest growth during the forecast period, driven by increasing investment in cathode regeneration, relithiation, and other processes designed to recover active materials with lower cost and energy requirements than conventional recycling routes.

Based on recycling process, the market is segmented into mechanical recycling, hydrometallurgical recycling, pyrometallurgical recycling, direct recycling, and hybrid recycling. Hydrometallurgical recycling currently represents the largest process segment owing to its established ability to recover lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and other materials at high purity and with greater selectivity than many conventional thermal processes. Direct recycling is expected to register the highest growth during the forecast period, supported by government-backed research, growing interest in lower-cost and lower-energy recovery routes, and the potential to regenerate cathode materials without fully breaking them down into base elements.

Based on battery type, the market is segmented into lithium-ion batteries, lead-acid batteries, nickel-based batteries, and emerging battery chemistries. Lithium-ion batteries currently account for the largest share of the market, driven by their dominant use in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, portable equipment, and energy storage systems. Emerging battery chemistries, including sodium-ion and solid-state batteries, are expected to register the highest growth during the forecast period as manufacturers and recyclers begin developing dedicated processing capacity for future feedstock volumes. The increasing diversity of lithium-ion chemistries, including NMC, NCA, LFP, LCO, and LMO, is also driving demand for flexible and chemistry-aware recycling equipment.

Based on battery form factor, the market is segmented into cylindrical cells, prismatic cells, pouch cells, battery modules, and battery packs. Battery modules and packs currently account for a significant share of demand because of their use in electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems and the need for safe discharge, dismantling, and material preparation before downstream processing. Cylindrical, prismatic, and pouch cells are expected to generate strong equipment demand as cell-level automation, pack disassembly, robotic handling, and chemistry-specific shredding systems become more widely adopted. The increasing variety of form factors is encouraging recyclers to deploy flexible equipment capable of processing mixed or variable feedstock.

Based on feedstock, the market is segmented into end-of-life batteries and manufacturing scrap. Manufacturing scrap currently accounts for the largest share of the market, reflecting substantial scrap volumes generated during gigafactory ramp-up, process qualification, yield improvement, and production expansion. End-of-life batteries are expected to register the highest growth during the forecast period as the first large wave of electric vehicle batteries deployed over the past decade begins reaching end-of-life. The combination of immediate manufacturing scrap and future end-of-life battery volumes is creating a two-stage expansion opportunity for recycling equipment suppliers.

Based on recovered material, the market is segmented into lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, copper, aluminum, and graphite. Lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese recovery currently represent important value pools because of their strategic role in cathode production and battery economics. Lithium recovery is expected to witness strong growth as battery manufacturers and policymakers prioritize domestic sources of battery-grade lithium and seek to reduce dependence on primary mining. Copper, aluminum, and graphite recovery are also gaining importance as recyclers improve the economics of mechanical separation and seek to maximize the value recovered from complete battery systems.

Based on capacity, the market is segmented into small-scale, medium-scale, large-scale, and gigafactory-scale systems. Large-scale and gigafactory-scale systems are expected to account for an increasing share of new equipment investment as battery manufacturers, automotive OEMs, and dedicated recyclers build high-throughput facilities. Small- and medium-scale systems remain relevant for regional collection, specialized processing, research, distributed recycling, and markets with limited feedstock concentration. The deployment of capacity-appropriate equipment is influenced by local battery volumes, transportation economics, feedstock consistency, safety requirements, and access to recovered-material markets.

The report also analyzes market performance across battery recycling companies, battery manufacturers, automotive OEMs, battery material producers, electronics manufacturers, energy storage system manufacturers, and waste management companies. Battery recycling companies currently account for the largest share of the market because they operate dedicated facilities processing feedstock from multiple upstream sources and provide specialized recovery services. Battery manufacturers are expected to register the highest growth during the forecast period as gigafactory operators increasingly integrate in-house or co-located recycling equipment to process manufacturing scrap and support closed-loop material strategies.

Regional Analysis

The report provides comprehensive market analysis across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and the Middle East & Africa. Regional evaluations consider electric vehicle adoption, battery manufacturing capacity, gigafactory construction, end-of-life battery volumes, critical-material availability, recycling regulations, government funding, closed-loop strategies, and investments influencing market growth.

Asia-Pacific currently accounts for the largest share of the global battery recycling equipment market, supported by the region's dominant position in battery cell manufacturing, electric vehicle production, energy storage deployment, electronics manufacturing, and battery materials processing. China, Japan, South Korea, and India are investing in battery recycling infrastructure to process manufacturing scrap and the growing installed base of lithium-ion batteries. The region's extensive battery supply chain, large electric vehicle market, high concentration of gigafactories, and established materials and equipment industries are generating sustained demand for shredding, sorting, black mass processing, hydrometallurgical, pyrometallurgical, direct recycling, and material-refining equipment.

North America is expected to register the fastest growth throughout the forecast period, driven by substantial government-backed investment in domestic battery manufacturing, recycling, critical-material recovery, and supply-chain localization. Public funding, tax incentives, recycling targets, electric vehicle adoption, and the development of new gigafactories are accelerating the buildout of domestic recycling infrastructure across the United States and Canada. The region's growing focus on closed-loop battery materials, local-content requirements, and recovery of lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, copper, aluminum, and graphite is expected to create significant opportunities for advanced equipment suppliers, recyclers, automotive OEMs, and battery manufacturers.

Europe continues to demonstrate robust growth driven by its expanding electric vehicle market, battery manufacturing investment, stringent recycling and sustainability requirements, and efforts to establish a circular battery economy. The region's regulatory emphasis on battery collection, producer responsibility, recycled content, material traceability, and carbon reduction is supporting demand for safe and efficient recycling equipment. Latin America is expected to present emerging opportunities as electric mobility, energy storage, mining, and battery-related infrastructure expand, particularly in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, and Chile. The Middle East & Africa are also expected to experience gradual growth as electric vehicle adoption, renewable energy storage, industrial development, and waste-management capabilities improve.

Competitive Landscape

The report presents a comprehensive evaluation of the competitive environment by examining the strategic positioning of leading market participants, their collection and discharge equipment, dismantling and robotic systems, crushing and shredding equipment, sorting and separation technologies, black mass processing systems, hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical platforms, direct recycling equipment, material recovery solutions, environmental and safety systems, partnerships, acquisitions, geographic expansion initiatives, research and development investments, and recent business developments.

Competitive benchmarking enables stakeholders to evaluate companies based on material recovery rates, processing throughput, equipment flexibility, chemistry compatibility, feedstock handling, safety performance, automation, energy efficiency, material purity, plant integration, service support, and global market presence. The study also analyzes how market participants are leveraging automated disassembly, machine vision, AI-based sorting, high-throughput shredding, hydrometallurgical processing, direct cathode regeneration, black mass refining, process control, and closed-loop system integration to strengthen their competitive positioning within the battery recycling equipment market.

Fully imported vehicles (CBUs) will face the highest tax rate, above the current ‌10 per cent excise ⁠tax, Pornchai Thiraveja ⁠said.

A lower tax rate will apply to vehicles imported ​for testing purposes and to those imported for local assembly or production, according ​to Pornchai.

Vehicles manufactured in Thailand with the use of local content will be subject to the lowest tax ​rate, he said.

A grace ⁠period will give ‌automakers time to adapt to the new ​tax regime, ​but its duration has yet to ⁠be determined.

title: Volvo Trucks' “lock and leave” software updates go live across North America
description:
Over six months, Volvo Trucks increased the share of its connected trucks running the latest software from 25% to more than 80%.
More than 7,500 updates were completed in August and Volvo Trucks’ connected systems can dispatch up to 20,000 software updates per day.
September 10, 2026 To learn more about Volvo Trucks North America, visit the company website.
For further information, please contact: Allison Scudder Public Relations Manager 336.833.4679 allison.scudder@volvo.com Volvo Trucks North America, headquartered in Greensboro, North Carolina, is one of the leading heavy-duty truck manufacturers in North America.
Volvo Trucks North America provides complete transport solutions for its customers, offering a full range of diesel, alternative-fuel and all-electric vehicles, and is part of the Volvo Trucks global organization.
text:
Drivers can now start a software update, lock the truck, and walk away, whether that is a 30-minute break or an overnight stop. The new capability enables trucks to stay current with the latest software without interrupting operations or requiring a visit to the dealership.

Through over-the-air software updates, remote diagnostics and predictive service capabilities, Volvo Trucks estimates that it has helped customers avoid more than 100,000 days of unplanned downtime, representing approximately $60 million in avoided costs. Over six months, Volvo Trucks increased the share of its connected trucks running the latest software from 25% to more than 80%. More than 7,500 updates were completed in August and Volvo Trucks’ connected systems can dispatch up to 20,000 software updates per day.

Keeping trucks current without interrupting operations

The all-new Volvo VNL and all-new Volvo VNR are the most connected trucks Volvo Trucks has built, with a 24-volt electrical architecture that expands the amount and quality of vehicle data available to support remote diagnostics, predictive maintenance and future product development.

The trucks can be continuously updated by receiving software improvements over the air after they leave the dealership. Over-the-air updates can optimize systems including engine performance, transmission and battery management without requiring a service appointment. Volvo trucks running the latest software experience 24% fewer unplanned stops, helping fleets maximize uptime and keep trucks on the road.

“Technology makes our customers operations more productive," said Peter Voorhoeve, president, Volvo Trucks North America. “As software plays a greater role in improving uptime, updating the software should be as easy and convenient as possible. Now a driver can lock and leave their truck while the update runs during a break and return to a truck that is up to date and ready to go to work.”

Data that keeps trucks moving

Volvo Trucks has more than 220,000 connected trucks operating across North America, providing data that helps the company identify potential issues before they result in unplanned stops. Advanced analytics detect patterns in fault codes, enabling more proactive maintenance and earlier diagnostics. This connectivity also enables technicians to pre-diagnose issues before a truck reaches the dealership, contributing to a 95% first-time fix rate.

“A connected truck keeps improving long after it leaves the dealership," said Nicole Portello, senior vice president and chief digital officer, Volvo Trucks North America. “The data coming from these trucks helps us identify where we can get ahead of a potential fault code today, while also giving our engineers insights that can help shape the next generation of Volvo trucks. For fleets, the goal is not simply more data, it is providing actionable information they can use to improve their operations.”

By combining over-the-air software updates, remote diagnostics and increasingly advanced connected services, Volvo Trucks is continuing to expand how software and vehicle data can help customers improve uptime and keep trucks operating at their best.
